<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 28 Oct 2026 23:04:50 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Mercedes bets on model blitz as China slump deepens]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/mercedes-bets-on-model-blitz-as-china-slump-deepens/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/mercedes-bets-on-model-blitz-as-china-slump-deepens/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 07:32:21 +0000Mercedes-Benz Group is pushing ahead with its biggest product and cost overhaul in years, betting it can restore profitability even as China turns from a growth engine into one of the biggest drags on the business.

Third-quarter revenue at the German carmaker fell 4.5 per cent to €30.7 billion, while adjusted group earnings before interest and tax declined 15 per cent, the group said on Wednesday.

The results came a day after Mercedes lowered its outlook, citing cost pressures and a drop in sales in the mainland.

Mercedes GLC review: A brilliant electric SUV that tries far too hard to get noticed

Chief executive Ola Källenius pointed to continued growth in Europe and the US as well as record electric-vehicle sales, as evidence that newer models are gaining traction. At the same time, he said market conditions had become “even more challenging”, particularly in China.

At its core cars division, adjusted earnings more than halved to €560 million in the third quarter, and the margin narrowed to 2.5 per cent from 4.8 per cent, reflecting the weaker contribution from China, as well as currency and product-launch costs.

Mercedes is counting on further product launches and lower costs to rebuild profitability, while stopping short in its statement of giving a timetable for a recovery in margins.

On Tuesday, Mercedes had said it was downgrading its outlook due to a deepening downturn in China and higher fourth-quarter costs, including more expensive materials. That triggered a 3.9 per cent slide in the shares, and brought the year-to-date loss to 34 per cent.

China has become the biggest obstacle to Källenius’s attempt to rebuild profitability. Mercedes vehicle sales there fell 31 per cent in the third quarter from a year earlier, extending a decline driven by weaker luxury demand, fierce price competition and increasingly sophisticated domestic rivals.

Mercedes-Benz issues birth certs for vintage cars

The pressure extends across Germany’s auto industry. BMW and Volkswagen have also warned that deteriorating conditions in China are hurting earnings, highlighting how quickly a market that once generated outsize profits has become one of the sector’s biggest structural problems.

Volvo chief executive Håkan Samuelsson said last week that the market for western-developed cars in China isn’t coming back.

For Mercedes, the reversal strikes at the heart of a strategy Källenius has pursued for years: selling fewer cars while concentrating on expensive models capable of generating higher margins. The S-class, Maybach, G-Class and AMG range have been central to that push, but the deterioration of China’s luxury-car market has made the equation increasingly difficult.

Mercedes is responding with cost cuts, including an effort to save about 8 per cent on materials versus 2024 levels, with even steeper targets in China.

Källenius is also shrinking an industrial footprint built for stronger volumes, as the company’s global passenger-car capacity declines. Voluntary redundancy programmes are being used to reduce the German workforce.

The other leg of the recovery plan is Mercedes’s biggest-ever product offensive. More than 40 new or refreshed models are due by the end of 2027. The electric CLA and GLC are already being rolled out, with new versions of the C-Class, S-class, GLE and GLS among the models intended to rebuild demand.

China is a key part of that offensive. Mercedes has accelerated local development and sourcing, while targeting sharply lower costs in the country. New China-specific vehicles include long-wheelbase versions of models such as the electric GLC. – Bloomberg

]]>Krisztian Bocsi<![CDATA[Markets subdued as earnings and oil prices weigh]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/28/markets-subdued-as-earnings-and-oil-prices-weigh/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/10/28/markets-subdued-as-earnings-and-oil-prices-weigh/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:14:42 +0000European ‌shares were subdued on Wednesday after several disappointing earnings reports, coupled with higher oil prices, exacerbated investor unease ahead of a rate decision from the European Central Bank (ECB).

Dublin

Bank of Ireland enjoyed a near 4 per cent bounce in its share value after it upgraded key financial targets for the year on the back of positive lending and deposits data. In trading update, chief executive Myles O’Grady said the further “positive commercial performance” had led the bank to upgrade its net interest income guidance.

Rival AIB was also up as were financials across Europe, closing the session 1.6 per cent ahead. PTSB traded broadly flat after the bank criticised an approach to buy it from Axis Capital in a High Court hearing to approve the proposed €1.6 billion acquisition of the bank by Austrian banking group Bawag.

Elsewhere Ryanair shares were down over 2 per cent as elevated oil prices and geopolitical uncertainty continue to weigh on the outlook for the sector.

London

UK shares closed subdued, as ‌gains in banks after a lower-than-feared levy in finance minister John Healey’s first budget were countered by declines in Unilever and GSK after their results failed to ​impress investors.

The blue-chip FTSE 100 index ended 0.1 per cent higher, while the midcap FTSE 250 reversed course to close 0.3 per cent lower. It had touched a near two-month high earlier in the session.

Banks provided the biggest boosts to the index, up 1.1 per cent. Shares of Lloyds Banking Group, NatWest and Barclays rose between 1 per cent and ​2 per cent after Healey announced a lower than feared temporary increase in the bank profit surcharge to 6 per cent.

UK betting firms also ​rose after Healey announced a smaller-than-expected gambling tax increase. Entain ​rose 3.6 per cent and Evoke rose 3.7 per cent after machine games duty was raised to 25 per cent from 20 per cent.

Among notable earnings, GSK dropped 4.8 per cent as ​its pipeline push and growth plans via a £1.9 billion cost-saving programme failed to convince ​investors.

Unilever fell 2.1 per cent after reporting softer results in its foods business, dragging the personal care, drug and grocery sector down nearly 1.4 per cent.

Europe

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index rose 0.07 per cent to 644.14 points with the media and mining indices among the biggest laggards.

Thyssenkrupp was the ⁠biggest individual loser on the Stoxx 600 with ​a 17 per cent decline, after a muted market debut for ​its materials trading division.

Dutch payments platform Adyen was the second biggest loser, down over 13 per cent after it lowered its core ‌earnings margin target for 2026.

Among financial stocks, Deutsche Bank gained about 4 per cent ⁠after reporting a surprise ​jump in third-quarter profit.

On the other hand, Spain’s Santander fell 5.6 per cent after third-quarter results as weaker earnings in Brazil weighed, leading the bank-heavy Spanish benchmark down 1.5 per cent, the most among peers.

UBS dipped 0.6 per cent after posting a third-quarter net profit roughly in line with expectations. However, analysts remained constructive on the sector.

Among other earnings, Stellantis added over 15 per cent after posting a slight increase in ​operating income in the third quarter, leading gains on the automobile index, which rose ​1.3 per cent.

New York

US stocks were choppy as weakness in megacaps such as Tesla and Apple offset chipmaker gains sparked by SK Hynix’s bumper results.

Memory chipmaker Micron Technology jumped 4.8 per cent to its highest in over two weeks after South Korean rival SK Hynix reported a more than sevenfold jump in quarterly profit. SK Hynix’s US-listed shares gained 12.2 per cent.

Limiting gains in main benchmarks, most ​megacap and growth stocks traded lower. Tesla dipped 1.3 per cent after surging more than 9 per cent in the last two sessions. Apple eased 0.5 per cent, while SpaceX dropped 2.4 per cent.

The focus now shifts to quarterly ​results from hyperscalers Microsoft and Alphabet, due after markets close on Wednesday, with both companies expected to report accelerating cloud growth. – Additional reporting by Reuters

]]>Michael Nagle<![CDATA[‘Steady as she goes’ UK budget fuels talk that bigger changes are in the wings]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/28/steady-as-she-goes-uk-budget-fuels-talk-that-bigger-changes-are-in-the-wings/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/28/steady-as-she-goes-uk-budget-fuels-talk-that-bigger-changes-are-in-the-wings/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:03:27 +0000“Is that it?” an indignant Tory leader Kemi Badenoch asked after the inaugural budget speech on Wednesday of Labour’s new chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey.

His boss, UK prime minister Andy Burnham, rose to power over the summer with a near-revolutionary promise to reverse 40 years of right-wing economic orthodoxy. Yet his chancellor’s first big fiscal set-piece was a studied exercise in treading water, more notable for what it didn’t do than what it did.

It included modest £100 cash rebates to council tax payers and VAT cuts on electricity, but there was no mention of how to cap galloping welfare spending, which is predicted to rise by more than £100 billion annually within the next five years.

In his low-key house of commons speech, Healey blamed the inflationary pressures of US president Donald Trump’s war in Iran for limiting his fiscal options. Nancy Pelosi, the former Democratic congressional leader, watched on, smiling, from the public gallery.

Yet as Healey assiduously avoided big decisions around welfare and also, possibly, future tax rises to plug budget gaps, bookmakers shortened their odds on an early British election despite Burnham’s repeated denials that one was on the cards.

“I don’t know how many times I’ve done this now, but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months,” Burnham told GB News on Wednesday. Not everyone was convinced: election chatter still cranked up in Westminster’s energetic rumour mill.

There were a few significant decisions buried in Healey’s budget. For the first time, he committed the UK to reaching 3 per cent defence spending (as measured against national income) by 2030. He said a £10 billion black hole in the UK defence investment plan would be filled by extra 1 per cent per year spending cuts by other departments.

Britain is a nation increasingly convinced it must prepare for a future war with Russia, for which its rickety armed forces are unprepared. The debate is usually pitched in Westminster as an imperative to cut welfare spending to fund new military equipment.

Healey kicked this can further down the road until his next spending review, which is unlikely to be before next autumn. He said the UK government wanted time to first consider reports it had commissioned on youth unemployment and disability payments, which are due next month.

In her two budget since Labour’s election win in 2024, Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves backloaded departmental spending cuts, with the worst of the pain not due to land until nearer the end of the current UK parliament in 2028 and 2029.

Healey left Reeves’ plan untouched in his budget speech on Wednesday, which further fed the early election rumours among Westminster observers unconvinced he would really be prepared to implement austerity in the run-up to a scheduled election.

Meanwhile, he persevered with a swathe of baffling, small measures, such as reduced tariffs on certain canned vegetable goods.

“The prime minister came to power promising to end 40 years of neoliberalism and instead we got 4p off gherkins,” said Badenoch.

]]>House of Commons<![CDATA[Fed holds US interest rates ahead of midterm elections]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/28/fed-holds-us-interest-rates-ahead-of-midterm-elections/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/28/fed-holds-us-interest-rates-ahead-of-midterm-elections/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:53:52 +0000The US Federal Reserve has kept interest rates on hold days before midterm elections even as the surge in fuel prices sparked by the Iran war reverberates across the world’s biggest economy.

Most of the rate-setters on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee of the US’s central bank on Wednesday said they needed “more information” before deciding what to do “to ensure a timely return of inflation” to their 2 per cent goal, after holding the federal funds rate within a range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent.

The decision to hold came after a 10-to-two vote, with two members favouring a quarter point rise in rates.

The committee acknowledged economic activity was “expanding at a strong pace”, signalling mounting concern the economy is in danger of overheating from the AI boom.

The decision, which was widely expected by Wall Street, comes despite fresh evidence that inflation is accelerating and spreading across the economy.

While the Fed says it does not take politics into account in its decisions, some economists said rate-setters would be reluctant to raise rates with the critical election that will determine control of Congress looming next Tuesday.

Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz and inflation in the US rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.

The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress.

Before Wednesday’s announcement, senior Fed officials hinted they were willing to wait and see what happened to price pressures before raising interest rates again.

The central bank increased rates for the first time in more than three years in September in an attempt to contain inflation. The decision defied Donald Trump’s attempts to press the central bank into drastically lowering rates.

Wall Street stocks slightly pared gains after the decision which shifts the probability of a rate hike to the Fed’s next monetary policy meeting in December.

“The Fed didn’t throw any curveballs,” said ​Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group in Omaha. “Likely ⁠the pressure will be to do one more hike in December, as inflation is ‌still ‌potentially ​an issue.”

Financial markets ⁠are pricing in an 86 per cent likelihood ⁠of a 25-basis-point rate ​hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December, up from 78.3 per cent on Tuesday, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026 / Reuters / Guardian service

]]>Saul Loeb<![CDATA[Brothers at loggerheads over decision to appoint director to building firm they own ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/brothers-at-loggerheads-over-decision-to-appoint-director-to-building-firm-they-own/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/brothers-at-loggerheads-over-decision-to-appoint-director-to-building-firm-they-own/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:42:09 +0000A dispute has broken out between the brothers who own the successful Glenman Corporation building company over the appointment of a third director to their two-man board, the High Court heard.

The two sides are already due in court in December for hearing of a shareholder oppression case.

Judge Brian Cregan on Wednesday granted an interim injunction to Micheál Conneally, one of the two owner-directors of Glenman, preventing his brother and majority shareholder, Albert Conneally, from appointing a third director.

The application was made by counsel Gary McCarthy on an ex parte, or one side only represented, basis.

Glenman Corporation Ltd was set up 33 years ago by the Conneallys, who built up a thriving building, contracting and civil engineering business in Ireland and Britain.

They initially worked on upgrading pubs, restaurants and churches, before developing housing projects and becoming one of the leading builders of schools in the 1990s and 2000s.

Albert holds 60 per cent of the shares and Micheál the other 40 per cent.

Differences arose between the brothers, and in 2023 Micheál brought shareholder oppression proceedings against his brother. Albert sought to have the case heard “in camera”, or in private, but this was rejected by the High Court in April 2024.

A hearing of the dispute began in October last year after mediation failed to produce a resolution. The hearing was adjourned to facilitate further mediation efforts, Micheál’s solicitor Peter Boyle said in an affidavit. These also failed to produce a resolution, and the case is now listed for hearing at the start of December.

Last Friday, Boyle said, Micheál received an email stating Albert wished to appoint a third director, David Issott, to the board. Under Section 194 of the Companies Act 2014, a majority shareholder can appoint a new director without having to convene a general meeting, the court heard.

Correspondence followed, and in one letter from Albert’s lawyers to Micheál’s lawyer, the suggestion that the appointment of Issott was an attempt to usurp Micheál’s rights was rejected.

“The prolonged inability to agree on matters of management, to put matters neutrally, has produced a structural impasse which is detrimental to the company,” the letter said.

It also said Micheál should “not be permitted to hold the company to ransom” during the proceedings by making a claim that the appointment of an independent and external director is somehow inappropriate.

Boyle said no opportunity had been given to Micheál to consider Issott’s nomination.

He also said Micheál had overseen the growth of UK business to the extent that it is now the only profitable arm. Albert, he said, had meanwhile overseen the demise of the Irish arm.

According to figures produced on behalf of Albert, turnover in the UK for 2025 was €32 million, while in Ireland it was €2.7 million.

Boyle said it was intolerable that Albert should continue to act in this manner, especially with the hearing of the oppression proceedings just four weeks away. The existing deadlock is likely to be addressed by that hearing, he said.

The judge said he was satisfied to grant the interim injunction restraining Albert and the company from proceeding to appoint a third director.

He said the case could return next week.

]]>Iryna Melnyk<![CDATA[PTSB attacks Axis in court over effort to disrupt Bawag’s €1.6bn takeover ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/ptsb-share-price-was-of-utmost-importance-in-ministers-decision-on-16bn-takeover-offer/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/ptsb-share-price-was-of-utmost-importance-in-ministers-decision-on-16bn-takeover-offer/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 18:29:52 +0000PTSB has in court attacked the approach of advisory group Axis, cofounded by former Bank of Scotland Ireland chief Mark Duffy, to try to disrupt the lender’s takeover by Austrian banking group Bawag.

Axis Capital is “nowhere near a position to make an offer” to rival the €1.6 billion offer from Bawag, the High Court has heard.

There was “no certainty’ that the firm’s offer of €3.20 a share, higher than Bawag’s €2.97 a share proposal, “can actually be made”, Kelley Smith, counsel for PTSB, told Judge Michael Quinn on the second day of legal proceedings to approve the proposed acquisition of the bank.

“Axis is a €100 micro-company,” she said, pointing to financial accounts for the year ended May 2026 that “showed €100 on its balance sheet”. Axis was cofounded by Duffy and Lutz Hartmann, a Frankfurt-based international lawyer.

“The company has no track record in M&A [mergers and acquisitions] transactions and, we would say, lacks the resources to actually implement an offer. We now see that, actually, it is not an offerer but it intends to be some form of arranger,” Smith said.

“Axis have waxed and waned on what they’d like the court to do,” Smith continued, and “the court should discourage such approaches” that “seek to disrupt” proceedings.

Duffy asked for “one minute” of Judge Quinn’s time.

“What has struck me since yesterday, particularly over the past few minutes, is that everyone is talking about the Bawag offer. There is at least one other offer – that comes from Axis,” he said.

The offer “is not speculative” and is supported by “one of the most esteemed investment banks in the world. We have a credible route to funding”, Duffy said. “And we are credible people, we have done many transactions in Ireland and globally”.

“We want access to information and limited time to consider this information,” he said in reference to the announcement last week that Axis Capital would seek an adjournment of up to six weeks.

Earlier in proceedings, the court heard from Des Carville, head of the shareholding and financial advisory division at the Department of Finance, on what led to Minister for Finance Simon Harris using the State’s 57.5 per cent stake in PTSB to support Bawag’s offer.

Share price was “of utmost importance”, Carville said, as it was “our primary driver to maximise value for the Irish taxpayer” when considering the State’s exit of its stake in the Irish banking sector.

Piotr Skoczylas, the managing director of Scotchstone Capital, which owns a less than 1 per cent stake in PTSB and is one of three shareholders objecting to the deal, asked Carville a series of questions on what formed “part of the Minister’s overall assessment to support the Bawag’s recommended cash offer”.

Small PTSB shareholders ‘paying for Minister’s exit’ in €1.6bn takeover deal, court hears

These included commercial matters, such as the bank’s branch footprint, and the Minister’s views of Bawag’s approach to the deal – for example, meeting trade union representatives.

Carville said these issues were not the Minister’s primary considerations. “Price was the first and foremost consideration,” he said. “Other points are secondary points; they flow from the transaction.

“It was a consequence of the offer by Bawag [that] the proposed transaction afforded the Minister the opportunity to exit his last remaining stake” in the bank, Carville said. “It was not a major part” of the Minister’s decision, he added, but “a small part of it”.

“We have resisted pressure from banks to sell shares” at times when the price on offer was not optimal, he said, and “it has taken us 13 years” to get to a point of satisfaction with a PTSB takeover bid.

“If price was not important to us, I would not have spent 13 years of my time working on this,” he said.

]]><![CDATA[Healey keeps bond markets onside in first UK budget ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/uk-to-hike-taxes-on-banks-to-pay-for-energy-bill-cuts/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/uk-to-hike-taxes-on-banks-to-pay-for-energy-bill-cuts/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 17:05:35 +0000British prime minister Andy Burnham’s Labour government succeeded in keeping skittish bond markets onside with its first budget, which raised taxes on banks and gambling to pay for cost of living measures such as cuts to energy bills.

After creeping up for months, Britain’s cost of borrowing on international markets fell slightly after the budget on Wednesday, the first delivered by John Healey who has replaced Rachel Reeves as chancellor of the exchequer.

As he rose to his feet in the house of commons, Healey insisted his inaugural budget would be “built on fiscal discipline”, echoing language previously used by Reeves.

He mostly delayed big decisions around cutting Britain’s ballooning welfare bill and funding investment in its decrepit armed forces. Healey did, however, increase Britain’s “fiscal headroom” buffer to £15 billion (€17.7 billion), which reassured bond traders who had been worried about rises in inflation and spending against a backdrop of weak growth in Britain.

Healey also said he would stick to his predecessor’s “fiscal rules” that have proved popular with City traders, including eschewing borrowing for day-to-day spending and ensuring UK debt falls when measured against the size of the economy.

“[The point of] today was to really avoid a Liz Truss ‌moment,” said Mike Bell, head of market strategy at BlueBay Asset Management.

“[Healey] has been successful. The headroom came in line with expectations. It doesn’t give gilt investors anything to panic about in the near term, which was the goal.”

]]>Colin Keegan<![CDATA[A 97-year-old woman faces €455,000 payment to Bank of Ireland over life loan taken out in 2003]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/27/life-loan-proves-a-millstone-for-97-year-old-pensioner/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/27/life-loan-proves-a-millstone-for-97-year-old-pensioner/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000I would like to draw your attention to a very serious issue involving a Bank of Ireland life loan to an elderly lady. I am hoping that by having this case highlighted it will help speed up our efforts to have the issue resolved, and also serve as a cautionary tale to anyone else considering taking on a life loan.

Back in 2003, when she was 72, a single woman with no children received correspondence from Bank of Ireland offering her a life loan. Having taken legal advice (she never discussed this advice with anyone), she took out a life loan of €130,000.

She actually only needed €30,000 at the time, so she put €100,000 back on deposit with Bank of Ireland, where it has remained ever since. (It is not clear why she took out €130,000 when she only needed €30,000.)

As of June this year, the total amount required to close the account was a staggering €455,081. The woman is now 97.

Her nieces and nephews have been trying unsuccessfully to get mediation on this loan with Bank of Ireland since 2022. A complaint was made in August last year to the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman (FSPO), but in a response in May this year, the ombudsman said it could be another 12-14 months before we hear from them on this complaint.

The general public needs to be more aware of the risks involved in life loans. While Bank of Ireland no longer offer such a product, there are ads for similar products from Spry Finance frequently aired on radio.

The behaviour of Bank of Ireland at all stages of this loan needs to be questioned and answers given.

The fact that the FSPO can tell a 97-year-old that it will be 12 to 14 months before a member of the investigative team will be appointed to this case is shocking.

JC

Any regular reader will know that while I accept life loans and similar equity release products can be useful for certain borrowers, my view is that they are very much credit of last resource – something you turn to only if you cannot raise money you need any other way.

They were, as you say, popular in the early years of this century and heavily marketed by the lenders offering them, including Bank of Ireland. They offered people who might be wealthy on paper due to the value of their home but cash poor – especially women with little or no pension cover – access to money that would not need to be repaid in their lifetime.

Lifeline or life sentence? How equity-release lifetime loans work

Interest built up over time and the loan was redeemed when you died or otherwise moved out of or sold the property. That interest could, and in some cases did, swallow up all the equity in a home. However, where the debt was greater than the eventual sale price, the bank committed not to chase the estate for any payment over and above the sale price.

The collapse of property prices saw them swiftly withdrawn from the market, alongside tracker loans, as banks faced the prospect of losing money on both products.

Your friend’s story is almost a textbook case study of what can go wrong.

Life loans were available only to those over the age of 65. People could borrow up to 20 per cent of the value of their homes if they were in their 60s to as much as 30 per cent for those in their 80s. For someone like your friend, borrowing at 72, the limit was 25 per cent.

The first alarm is that, as you tell it, she never proactively sought this loan; instead, she was simply targeted with marketing material by the bank.

What are your options if you want to release wealth tied up in your home?

This was certainly not unusual back in the wild west of the early noughties in the credit markets. People regularly got letters at that time telling them they had been pre-approved for loans they had never sought and found their credit card borrowing limits had been increased without any contact from or with them.

Was any of this ethical, including love-bombing a pensioner with offers of “easy-to-access” money? In my view, certainly not.

Does it amount to mis-selling? I’m certainly not going to second-guess the ombudsman when it comes to that. The FSPO is an office with far more resources and expertise than me, as well as long experience with such cases and clear lines of communication with the very top echelons of lenders such as Bank of Ireland.

But there are features of your friend’s story that are deeply concerning. While the woman was obliged under the terms of the loan to consult a solicitor – who had to sign forms to confirm their engagement – the bank also had a duty of care to ensure that it was selling appropriate products to people.

The fact that €100,000 of this €130,000 borrowed never moved from the deposit account into which it was lodged at Bank of Ireland should have raised alarm bells with the bank.

Bank of Ireland notes that, as in this case, it could be decades before repayment fell due. Interest on your friend’s loan has been building up for 25 years.

Equity release borrowing by older homeowners jumps 30% to €75m

“To ensure customers would understand the product, the information provided clearly explained the terms of the loan,” a spokesman for Bank of Ireland says. And, having read the product brochure, those terms should be very clear to anyone who took the time to read it in full. It is not hidden in seven-point type.

“Most importantly,” the bank continues, “before any life loan was agreed it was a requirement for each customer to obtain independent legal advice – and to show that they had taken that legal advice – to ensure that customers fully understood the terms and conditions.”

Whatever about Bank of Ireland mis-selling this loan, there are questions about the advice any legal practitioner gave this woman back in 2003. She clearly did not “need” this money – or most of it anyway – as €100,000 has sat untouched on deposit ever since, effectively losing value. It is just such a bad call on so many levels.

So what “advice” the solicitor provided, I have no idea. I can see them saying they advised only on the legal and contractual issues rather than the wisdom of taking the loan but that seems a very narrow and unhelpful interpretation of their role.

Reader’s attempts to foil fraudsters hit weird Bank of Ireland roadblock

The bank certainly appears to be sticking to its view that the loan has worked exactly as it should and as it was advised to the client. Whether that passes muster with the ombudsman remains to be seen, especially given she borrowed money under this expensive product that she clearly did not need. How was that assessed?

As for the ombudsman, I have sympathy. Asking a 97-year-old to hold on for up to 14 months to hear if they have a case certainly seems insensitive but the resources of the ombudsman are limited and all the cases that get to the investigation stage have people who are feeling hard done by, so how can they prioritise other than first come, first served.

It is simply unfortunate that it took so long for the details of this loan to emerge so that her extended family could help her.

]]><![CDATA[Actually, someone is to blame for the €125m in insurance claims written off by hospitals: consultants ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/actually-someone-is-to-blame-for-the-125m-in-insurance-claims-written-off-by-hospitals-consultants/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/28/actually-someone-is-to-blame-for-the-125m-in-insurance-claims-written-off-by-hospitals-consultants/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 06:00:01 +0000The news that public hospitals wrote off €125 million in unpaid debts from private health insurance companies over the last four years speaks to pretty much everything that is wrong with the health service. For a bit of context, €125 million would get 25,000 hip replacements, or pay the wages of about 2,000 nurses. It would only get you 5 per cent of a national children’s hospital.

First and foremost, it highlights the extent to which the public system is the loser in the incestuous relationship between public hospitals and private medicine, which has developed over the years, allowing publicly employed consultants to see private patients in public hospitals and avail of facilities funded by the State.

It has proved lucrative for the medical profession, which is not without influence. Thus the arrangement is very hard to dismantle – as demonstrated by the recent row over public consultants continuing to carry out private work in Dublin’s Rotunda Hospital. Somehow, this privilege has come to be seen as a sort of birthright for aspiring Irish consultant doctors.

The fact that this practice continues at Irish hospitals is hard enough to understand, but the idea that the hospitals in question are not billing the health insurance companies that make the whole thing supposedly viable is beyond comprehension.

The precise reason for public hospitals’ failure to collect the €125 million they are owed has not been elucidated. But the public accounts committee says that, according to the HSE, the number one reason is: “Consultants not completing the claim form on a timely basis, and [the] insurer refuses to process the claim as it has exceeded their allowable time for claim submission.”

According to Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill, no one in particular is to blame. “The consultant has to make sure to sign it [the claim] within a year. It has to be processed by the hospital and the HSE, and the insurance company has to pay it,” she has said.

Her insouciance about the failure of consultants to facilitate their hospital to collect bills incurred on their behalf at the cost of taxpayers is somewhat at odds with the vigour with which the Minister pursued the issue of public-only consultants carrying out private work in public hospitals earlier this year.

Consultants’ private healthcare in public settings has ‘ceased’, HSE review finds

Carroll MacNeill said she did not want to “ascribe fault” in the case of unclaimed insurance payments. “It’s everybody’s responsibility. But if there’s anybody there who hasn’t discharged their responsibility on that today, well, they really should because they really must.”

The health service is not noted for its efficiency, but when the minister of the day is reduced to asking people who work for her – consultants and others – to please do their job out of some sort of sense of duty or personal responsibility, you really have to wonder what is going on.

It’s unclear how much, if any, of the €125 million relates to VHI, but a failure to pay public hospitals on its part would be unsporting, to put it mildly

It is very hard to imagine the boss of a private sector company not wanting to apportion responsibility for a failure to collect €125 million, and instead just asking everybody involved to try a little harder in future.

The private health insurers are not exactly blameless either. Health insurance is big business in Ireland. Almost one in every two people has a policy, which is well above European norms. In Europe, the model tends towards State funding or mandatory public health insurance. In many ways, the Irish private health insurance industry is the yin to the yang of the tradition of allowing private medicine to be carried out in public hospitals.

Rotunda Hospital’s clash with Coalition over private maternity care deepens

The largest player in the market, with an almost 50 per cent share of it, is the VHI, which is owned by the State. A commercial body, it operates at arm’s length from the Government, and competes with privately owned insurers. Unlike other State companies, it does not pay a dividend, and retains any surplus that it makes.

It’s unclear how much, if any, of the €125 million relates to VHI, but a failure to pay public hospitals on its part would be unsporting, to put it mildly. It would also find themselves on common ground with all the other vested interests who seem to take the view that the taxpayer-funded health service is some sort of fatted calf.

‘I felt nobody had my back’: What the Rotunda row says about public v private maternity care

Something will have gone seriously wrong if VHI seems happy to go along with unnecessary losses being foisted on taxpayers because consultants – whose fees it also pays – appear to be unbothered about doing paperwork.

One useful exercise VHI and its peers could carry out – and perhaps share the results of with the Public Accounts Committee – is whether consultants adopt an equally dilettantish approach to putting in the paperwork to ensure their own fees are paid.

Linking the two might solve the problem.

]]><![CDATA[Pension or the new investment account: where should your spare cash go?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/28/pension-or-the-new-investment-account-where-should-your-spare-cash-go/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/28/pension-or-the-new-investment-account-where-should-your-spare-cash-go/Wed, 28 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Do you have spare cash sitting on deposit? If so, there’s a strong case for taking advantage of generous pension tax relief. But with a new Government-backed personal investment account set to open next July, are your spare savings better off going there instead?

Irish households had a whopping €175 billion sitting in low-interest bank accounts in the first six months of 2026, says the Central Bank. By leaving more than you need on deposit below the rate of inflation, the value of your money is shrinking. There are definitely better things to do with it.

Putting your spare cash towards an additional voluntary contribution (AVC) to your pension or into the new personal investment account (PIA) are both good ideas. But, before you move a cent, which is best for you?

Pension play

An AVC lets you add extra funds to your pension, topping up the regular contributions you and your employer make. Not only is this boosting your retirement savings, but you’ll get significant tax relief too.

“AVCs are among the most powerful, yet underutilised ways for Irish employees to build personal wealth,” says Niall O’Connor, founder of Financial Planning Matters.

The tax relief is most generous for higher earners. A single person earning €44,000 a year or more will benefit from 40 per cent tax relief on contributions.

Put €100 into your pension, for example, and the full €100 goes into your pot, where it can grow and compound tax-free, and the Government will give you €40 back. So, your €100 contribution costs you just €60.

Lower rate taxpayers get 20 per cent tax relief on contributions.

“You can effectively turn €6,000 of your own money into €10,000 invested towards retirement,” says O’Connor of higher rate taxpayers.

“This is a considerable advantage, before the investment has earned a single cent.”

It’s important to understand the age-related pension contribution limits within which you qualify for the tax relief.

If you’re aged 30 to 39, for example, you can contribute up to 20 per cent of your income and be eligible for the tax relief. This rises to 25 per cent for those aged 40 to 49, 30 per cent for those aged 50-54, jumping to 35 per cent for those aged up to 59 and 40 per cent for those aged over 60.

This is based on eligible earnings up to a ceiling of €115,000.

Importantly, the limits include your existing pension contributions. Take the example of a 40-year-old on €80,000 who already contributes 6 per cent of their salary to pension.

“The maximum personal contribution qualifying for tax relief would be €20,000,” says O’Connor. “Having already contributed €4,800, they could make an AVC of up to €15,200.”

They could contribute more, but they won’t get tax relief on anything over the 25 per cent limit for their age.

As a higher rate 40 per cent taxpayer, they make a tax saving at 40 per cent on their contribution so that €15,200 going into their pension only costs them €9,120. Revenue will give them a refund of €6,080, says O’Connor.

The upfront tax refund on an AVC is hard to beat, and your money can also benefit from tax-free investment growth within the pension as your money compounds in the years ahead.

If that €15,200 AVC remained invested over 25 years, assuming a 5 per cent annual investment return after charges, it could grow to approximately €51,500, says O’Connor.

Similarly, for someone aged 50 earning €100,000 who is already contributing 8 per cent of salary to their pension, their remaining personal contribution limit qualifying for relief would be 22 per cent of their salary, or €22,000.

After tax relief, contributing €22,000 to their pension only costs them €13,200.

Pension investments can go up or down of course but invested for 15 years at an illustrative 5 per cent annual return after charges, that single €22,000 contribution could grow to approximately €45,700, says O’Connor.

Money saved in a deposit account comes from your after-tax income, meaning you’ve already paid tax on those earnings and receive no additional tax relief for saving them, says Nick Charalambous, managing director of Alpha Wealth.

Keep €10,000 on deposit earning 2 per cent interest and it would generate just €134 a year once 33 per cent deposit interest tax is deducted.

With inflation running at 4 per cent, the cost of living is rising faster than the interest you are earning, so savings are actually losing purchasing power, says Charalambous.

“Watching your bank balance grow doesn’t necessarily mean you are building wealth.”

Having some accessible savings is essential of course. Don’t put your emergency fund or money for short-term goals into your pension.

“It makes little financial sense if you subsequently find yourself having to borrow at 7 or 8 per cent to fund another financial priority,” he says.

Personal investment account

Think of the Government’s new personal investment account as complementary to pension saving, not a replacement for it, says Charalambous.

Due to launch next July, you will be able to put up to €12,000 a year into the account, with a 1 per cent tax kicking in on any amount above the €50,000 tax-free threshold.

Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work

Lodge the full €12,000 and, unlike a pension contribution, you will not get anything back now from Revenue by way of tax relief. Any gains will, however, be able to grow without capital gains tax, exit tax or dividend withholding tax.

How much could your money grow? As with a pension, there are no guarantees. The S&P 500, which tracks the top 500 listed US companies, has returned about 6-8 per cent on an inflation-adjusted basis every year over the past 20 years.

There have been periods of downturn, however, so if you need to cash in your investment when markets are down, you do face the risk of losing your money.

Both pension and the PIA can offer tax-efficient investment growth, says O’Connor, but the mechanisms differ.

Pension funds generally benefit from tax-free investment growth while your money remains within the pension, with taxes applied when benefits are taken.

Under the proposed PIA, there is no tax on investments under the €50,000 threshold but a 1 per cent annual charge would apply on any amount over that.

This could mean paying tax on the account in years when your investment is losing money, simply because the overall balance exceeds €50,000.

“For somebody paying 40 per cent income tax, with sufficient unused pension contribution capacity and money genuinely intended for retirement, I would generally examine the AVC opportunity first because of the immediate tax relief available,” says O’Connor.

But once you’ve got your pension on track, the PIA could provide an attractive additional vehicle for accumulating wealth outside the pension system, he says.

Taxing times

Getting 40 per cent tax relief on pension contributions on the way in is great, but won’t I pay tax at 40 per cent when I take the money in retirement? Financial advisers get asked this all the time, says O’Connor.

It’s possible to get the 40 per cent income tax relief on your pension contribution and draw income from the pot in retirement without paying tax at the 40 per cent rate, says O’Connor.

Under current rules, you can generally draw down a quarter of your fund at retirement as a tax-free lump sum. The first €200,000 of qualifying retirement lump sums received over an individual’s lifetime is free of income tax. The next €300,000 is generally taxed at 20 per cent, he says.

The income tax rate you pay after that depends on how much you draw down from your fund each year.

Take a single retiree aged 66 who has €500,000 invested in an approved retirement fund (ARF) and is getting the maximum State pension, equivalent to about €15,564 a year.

If they withdraw 4 per cent of the ARF annually, or €20,000, this gives them a total retirement income of €35,564. That is below the €44,000 threshold this year for higher-rate income tax, says O’Connor. That threshold rises next year to €46,500.

Even someone with a €700,000 ARF who is withdrawing 4 per cent annually, or €28,000 a year when combined with the State pension, would have approximately €43,564 a year, still below the threshold for higher income tax.

These figures do assume the person has no other sources of taxable retirement income, such as a separate defined benefit or foreign pension, rental income or other investment withdrawals, he says.

Biggest difference to your pension pot is not how much money you put in

Accessibility

Another big difference when choosing between the AVC and the PIA for spare cash is accessibility, says Charalambous.

“The PIA’s main attraction is greater flexibility, allowing people to invest for medium- to long-term goals, without having to wait until retirement to access their money,” he says.

This will make it more attractive to those wanting to accumulate wealth for things other than retirement.

The fact that an investment receives favourable tax treatment does not automatically make it right for you.

“I would never recommend transferring all available cash into a pension simply to generate a tax refund,” says O’Connor.

How big should your pension pot be for a comfortable retirement in Ireland?

Before deciding what to do, identify three categories of money, he says: what you need available in the short term; what should be invested for medium- and long-term objectives; and what can be committed to retirement.

The PIA may become an attractive option for the second category, while AVCs can be particularly powerful for the third.

I need help tracking down a lost pension from my first job nearly 50 years ago

Use it or lose it

If you do have spare cash and you haven’t yet maxed out your pension contributions, don’t wait for the PIA to launch before acting, says Charalambous.

Pension tax relief is linked to the year – so use it or lose it.

“The mistake is missing an opportunity to claim valuable pension tax relief now while waiting for a scheme that hasn’t launched yet,” he says.

To claim tax relief against your earnings for last year (2025), an AVC must be made by October 31st of the current year.

There is an extended deadline of November 18th for Revenue Online Service (ROS) users such as those self-employed or tax agents handling self-assessed income tax.

“I would strongly encourage people to review their pension before the tax deadline. The tax advantages are simply too valuable to overlook,” says Charalambous.

You’ll need to act fast to claim pension relief against your 2025 earnings.

To make an AVC, first check how much unused personal pension contribution capacity remains for 2025, says O’Connor. Payroll or your pension provider should be able to tell you this.

Call Revenue and ask about your actual income tax position for 2025. Not everyone will qualify for 40 per cent tax relief on every euro contributed, even if they are generally considered a higher-rate taxpayer, he says.

Third, confirm you have sufficient cash to fund the contribution in the short term before any refund is received.

Fourth, think about how you want the pension AVC to be invested – in the same way as your payroll contributions or differently?

Making the contribution involves filling out a form, available through your pension provider’s website and a clearly labelled bank transfer to your pension provider’s account number on the form.

Pensions: In pursuit of financial security ... although chilly reality awaits

Choice

Any Government initiative to encourage Irish people to invest more rather than to continue stockpiling cash on deposit is a good thing but think of AVCs and PIAs as apples and oranges. They serve two different purposes.

But provided you have enough accessible funds to serve your short-term needs, either option is preferable to holding your wealth in cash deposits, says O’Connor.

For a lot of taxpayers, in the long term, it will probably be more tax efficient to maximise tax relief on pension contributions before contributing to an investment account.

“But for someone who has already maximised their pension contributions, or who wants to build investments they can access before retirement, it could be an attractive addition to their financial plan,” says Charalambous.

It warned that they could face fines and court appearances unless they display clearly what costs consumers are likely to face for all elements of their purchase.

In 2002, a tax was attached to plastic bags which currently stands at 22 cent.

There was some reluctance in the early days, but the tax was quickly embraced and after its introduction there was a dramatic reduction in the number of discarded plastic bags across the State.

In the year before the levy was rolled out, plastic bags made up as much as 5 per cent of the litter in Ireland, compared with less than 0.3 per cent now. The levy was revenue neutral with all the money raised going back into environmental measures.

Supermarkets subsequently phased out the so-called single-use plastic bags and have been charging more than 70 cent for heavier-duty plastic bags. The advantage for these is that bags that cost over 70 cent incur no levy, which means the shops make money on every single bag they sell.

The CCPC said that consumers have been contacting its helplines “indicating that there is no display signage in store or around the checkout area showing the price of shopping bags for sale”.

Under consumer law, retailers must clearly display prices for items being sold. These prices must be unambiguous, easily identifiable, clearly legible and on or near the product.

The CCPC said that where “breaches of the law are detected, [it] may take further action to ensure retailers comply with price display laws and consumers are properly informed when shopping. These actions range from the issuing of fixed payment notices and compliance notices up to prosecution in the courts.

“Retailers must comply with consumer law, and consumers have a right to know the price of any product they purchase, including shopping bags,” said the watchdog’s director of communications and consumer information, Aoibhín de Búrca.

“They should not be put on the spot at the till to pay it or notice it afterwards on their receipts.”

]]>Gareth Fuller<![CDATA[How Irish businesses operating in both the North and South face ‘unnecessary’ barriers]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/businesses-that-export-cross-border-are-more-profitable-more-resilient/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/businesses-that-export-cross-border-are-more-profitable-more-resilient/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 06:00:00 +0000Crá, the successful Irish language TV detective series telling the story of a garda and a podcaster’s investigation into the discovery of a body in a bog in Donegal, tells us much about changing patterns in cross-Border trade.

]]>NurPhoto<![CDATA[Inheritance taxes: what your family needs to know about recent changes]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/27/inheritance-taxes-what-your-family-needs-to-know-about-recent-changes/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/27/inheritance-taxes-what-your-family-needs-to-know-about-recent-changes/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 05:59:00 +0000It may not have been much, but earlier this month, a number of changes were made to Ireland’s inheritance tax regime, which may ease the burden – somewhat – on families when they look to pass on the family home and other assets.

So, what else might you need to know about changes to the inheritance, or capital acquisitions tax (CAT) regime?

Receipts on the rise

There is no doubt that the amount of CAT being collected by the Exchequer is on the rise, with the total yield surpassing €1 billion last year for the first time. This is more than double what was collected back in 2020. And inheritance tax is one of the main drivers of this, with some €968.4 million collected in 2025, up from €430.6 million in 2020, according to Revenue statistics.

More people are paying it, too. Figures show that 15,200 people paid the charge in 2025, up from 14,006 in 2024; 13,055 in 2023; and 11,376 in 2020. That’s a 25 per cent increase since 2020.

However, while there may be continued calls to increase the parent-to-child threshold further, the figures show that the biggest contributors to inheritance tax are those who leave money to relatives other than their children. The threshold for an aunt leaving money to a nephew or niece is quite low, at just €44,000. This means that a lot of the tax collected comes from this cohort – and it is on the rise.

As the table shows, so-called group B inheritances now account for 46 per cent of all receipts, compared with 41 per cent for parent-to-child transactions.

Did the changes go far enough?

The increase in the parent-to-child threshold of €20,000, or 5 per cent, will mean that someone inheriting €420,000 today, as opposed to before the budget, will save €6,600 in taxes. Group B, for transfers between relatives, also increased, from €40,000 to €44,000.

But is this enough?

Carl Donnelly is head of tax with accountancy and business advisory firm Cronin. He would have liked the Government to go further with the changes.

“It hasn’t really done enough in terms of where property prices are now,” he says, noting the continued increase in house prices. Today, for example, the median national price is €400,000 – or as much as €685,000 in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown.

As Donnelly puts it, a child inheriting a three-bedroom house in Dublin, with a few thousand in savings, is going to “to end up a good bit over the threshold”, which will mean facing a tax bill.

He would like to see the parent-to-child exemption moved closer to €500,000 (this level was in fact last exceeded in 2009, when the threshold rose to €542,544), or for the introduction of some sort of exemption on the family home.

Biggest benefit

Those who stand to benefit the most from the latest changes are families who can avail of either CAT business relief or agricultural relief. This is because once certain conditions are met, these reliefs reduce the taxable value of the asset for gifts or inheritances by 90 per cent.

As Donnelly notes, if you have a parent passing on shares in a company or land that’s eligible for relief and is worth €4.2 million, its taxable relief will drop to €420,000 thanks to the relief.

“The €20,000 increase in the threshold actually allows for €200,000 worth of value to transfer tax free,” he says. “That’s kind of where the main benefit is. It can be quite useful”.

Home or savings

For typical families, however, the changes don’t amount to a lot.

“It’s better than nothing but it’s not a huge amount, and it’s not going to be life changing for families,” says Donnelly.

Alison McHugh, partner and head of private client tax services at EY, agrees that the increases were “relatively modest and are unlikely to fundamentally alter estate or succession planning strategies”.

However, she adds that they are nevertheless “a welcome development”, adding that they will at least help to mitigate the impact of asset price inflation, particularly in relation to family homes and business assets.

“For a family with four children and 10 grandchildren, this will allow an additional €120,000 of value to fall outside of the charge to Irish CAT,” she says.

There was increasing pressure before the budget to increase this by a substantial amount, given claims that the existing regime discriminated against single and childless people. However, the 10 per cent increase is unlikely to offer such relief.

“For example, if you have no children but wish to split your estate between 10 nieces and nephews, this will allow you to give an additional €4,000 to each one, or €40,000 of value overall.”

One possible way to offer more relief is to allow a family home to be passed on tax free – no matter to whom it is transferred.

“It would alleviate a lot of concerns that childless homeowners have if the family home could pass tax free,” Donnelly says.

“It can cause a bit of stress,” says Donnelly, noting that someone might inherit in August, and have to pay the bill by the middle of November − a short time frame in which to come up with such an amount, even if the intention is to sell the property.

Changing rates

An aspect of the recent budget that may have surprised was the decision to reduce capital gains tax to 31 per cent but to leave CAT at 33 per cent.

As Donnelly notes, if parents transfer a home to a child today, a CGT bill might arise on this transfer, while the child might face CAT, depending on their thresholds and the value of the property. This CGT can be used to offset the CAT charge but now they are being charged at different rates.

While “it’s probably rare that they’d equal each other,” Donnelly says, he adds that he’s surprised nonetheless that they don’t track each other.

“That’s something that might change next year,” he says, adding that, ideally, CAT would fall right back to 20 per cent, the rate it was at before the 2008 banking and property crash.

Small gifts

One area in which many would have liked to see change is the small gifts exemption. This has stayed at the €3,000 level for quite some time, and no change was made in the budget. It allows someone to receive a gift of €3,000, tax free, each year, from anyone. “It would be great to see an increase in the small gift exemption as it has been €3,000 for a long time,” says McHugh. She adds that if this was increased to, say, €5,000, it could have a significant impact in allowing families to transfer wealth “in a more measured way but at a reduced tax cost”.

“It would also be helpful to families with no children as they could benefit a number of family members over a longer period of time at a significantly lower tax cost,” she says.

Donnelly agrees that the lack of a change was “very disappointing”.

“It’s a useful way for people to pass on bits of wealth,” he says.

So RTÉ is well used to unfavourable, and often unfair, comparisons. Unfair because the differences of scale are enormous, and with them come reservoirs of creative talent and technical resources that were always impossible to match on this side of the Irish Sea.

Still, having such a neighbour has generally been good news for anyone who cares about quality and editorial independence at RTÉ, because it offered a benchmark against which Montrose could be measured.

Less often compared is how the two countries’ political systems manage their relationship with public service broadcasting. That is even less flattering, and the same excuses do not apply.

The UK has far more rigorous and transparent structures for deciding what its national broadcaster is for and how to pay for it. Chief among them is the royal charter, renewed every decade after intense scrutiny and debate at Westminster. Ireland’s approach is ramshackle, as this month’s shambolic budget handling of RTÉ’s funding demonstrated.

Income from ‘broken’ television licence fee down €5.7m in first nine months

We are now on the cusp of an alignment as rare as a total solar eclipse. Both governments face the same deadline for deciding how to pay for public service broadcasting and make it fit for the mid-21st century. The BBC’s current charter expires on December 31st, 2027. So does the three-year funding deal struck for RTÉ in 2024.

In London, the process began last December with a green paper canvassing everything from modest licence fee reform to advertising and a premium subscription tier, followed by a public consultation and a lengthy House of Commons committee inquiry.

In Dublin, we had the Future of Media Commission, whose recommendation on funding was rejected. Whether that recommendation was wise is debatable, but it hardly justifies the procrastination that has followed.

In the UK, these questions are argued over in parliament, on a timetable fixed by the charter. In Ireland, they are settled, or not, in irate correspondence between departments, while a toothless Oireachtas committee goes in search of soundbites. Neither country faces an easy decision but, despite all its problems, the BBC is starting from a much better place.

One reason is that the UK licence fee rises with inflation under the current funding settlement and now stands at £180 (€212). The Irish fee, frozen at €160 for 18 years, would be about €195 had it kept pace with prices.

Last year, RTÉ received €183.5 million from the licence fee and €41.3 million directly from the exchequer. Indexation would have brought in roughly €40 million more, almost exactly the size of that top-up. Most of the so-called bailout was simply the cost of political reluctance to grasp that political nettle.

And that assumes the precipitous fall in licence sales still happened. There, too, the contrast is stark. Between 2022 and 2025, UK licences in force fell by about 4 per cent. In Ireland, sales fell by 19 per cent over the same period. Whether through evasion or households abandoning traditional TV, every lost licence hits the bottom line.

Only about four in 10 Irish households now buys a licence. Strip out those with no television, and the half a million or so with State-funded free licences, and somewhere between a quarter and two-fifths of those legally obliged to pay do not.

A household charge at the current rate, levied on everyone not entitled to a free licence, would raise roughly €90 million to €115 million a year more than the existing system, allowing for a reduction in the current €160 price. Richard Bruton in 2019 promised such a charge to arrive by 2024. It never did.

UK culture secretary Lisa Nandy and her Irish counterpart Patrick O’Donovan face essentially the same problems. But O’Donovan’s are far worse and that, for all RTÉ’s faults, owes less to the broadcaster than to the short-termism and procrastination of successive Irish governments.

A universal media charge would be politically unpopular and is regarded by some as regressive. It is far from clear that the organisations themselves have the capacity to remain relevant in the post-broadcast age.

Elsewhere in Europe, stocks across the Continent saw steady growth as the trading week began, although the results of the Brazilian presidential election ricocheted across national economies on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean.

Shares in Santander bank slid 3.24 per cent downwards by close of markets as the Spanish financial institution, whose primary subsidiary outside of Europe is located in Brazil, reckoned with the re-election of left-wing Lula da Silva over far-right Jair Bolsonaro.

Meanwhile, Portuguese energy provider Galp Energia suffered larger losses, with its share price plummeting 10.84 per cent, in some part due to the uncertainty of its linguistic neighbour, but also the collapse of merger talks with Madrid-based energy company Moeve.

France’s luxury industry somewhat recuperated last week’s declines, as Hermès grew its share price 3.31 per cent by close, following a poor week of trading due to lower-than-expected financial results being published.

New York

Early trades on Wall Street were bolstered by renewed confidence from investors in AI stock and brief respite from soaring oil prices.

Before midday New York time, the Nasdaq 100 index jumped some 1.25 per cent, while the S&P 500 hovered about 0.75 per cent up from Friday’s close of market price point and the Dow Jones Industrial Average trailed behind, rising 0.20 per cent or so.

As US officials and representatives from their allies in the Middle East traveled to Iran in a bid to defuse rising tensions, the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil (the industry benchmark) fell below $115, having soared last week to levels not seen since May.

Anthropic, the AI programmers behind the Claude chatbot, released its prospectus earlier in the day, detailing the exponential growth that has led it to a $965 billion valuation in its latest private funding round in May. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg.

]]>Michael Nagle

A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.

The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.

The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.

While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.

Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.

The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.

 

The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.

Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.

Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.

An observation deck at the top of the EU's tallest building, Varso Tower in Warsaw, has opened to the public.

Located 230m up on the tower's 53rd floor, the attraction offers a 360° panorama of Poland's capital.https://t.co/VeEapOmh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2025

The result is an incredible level of explorable detail, from major landmarks, such as the communist-era Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower, the EU’s tallest building, down to the seating steps and bars along the Vistula River boulevards.

The map also features graveyards reflecting Warsaw and Poland’s diverse past, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish and Tatar Muslim graves. Around 1 November, when Poles visit cemeteries around All Saints’ Day, candles glow around the graves.

A final touch Yildirim has added is a flight simulator, allowing users to travel over the city – and complete missions – in a Cessna aeroplane, an air ambulance, a flying car, or even a UFO that takes off from the Copernicus Science Centre and travels to the National Stadium.

I turned Warsaw into a flight sim 🛩️

Take off from Chopin, fly through the ring over the Palace of Culture, then land a UFO inside Stadion Narodowy as the roof opens 🛸

Desktop only for now. Can you land it? 👇 pic.twitter.com/DT2fdk1Vem

— Bedirhan (@bedcodes) October 27, 2026

Speaking to Notes from Poland, Yildirim says that he moved to Poland in 2022 to pursue a job in IT before starting his own business. Initially living in Kraków, the country’s second-largest city, he then moved to Warsaw in 2025.

Asked what his own personal favourite places in the city are, Yildirim points to Warsaw’s parks, such as Skaryszewski, Pole Mokotowskie and Łazienki. His favourite neighbourhood is Saska Kępa on the right bank of the Vistula.

The software engineer adds that his project is an example of how AI can be an “amazing tool to do 90% of the job very quickly”. The remaining 10% of human input “is what keeps it from being ‘AI slop'”.

Yildirim says that, without the use of AI, the map of Warsaw he created would have needed an entire team to build over a period of months.

Poland has detained a Ukrainian citizen who is wanted by Romania on suspicion of involvement in an arson attack on a defence company carried out on behalf of Russia.

On Tuesday, the Polish police’s Central Investigation Bureau (CBŚP) announced that anti-terrorism officers had detained the man, who can be named only as Artem S. under Polish privacy law, in Warsaw under a European Arrest Warrant issued by Romania.

In the early hours of 14 September, a fire broke out in the city of Brașov, Romania, in the immediate vicinity of premises belonging to Carfil, a manufacturer of military equipment. Carfil is a subsidiary of ROMARM, a state-owned defence company.

On Monday this week, the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) said it had determined that the fire had been deliberately caused by a “sabotage network coordinated from Russia”. It added that “several citizens of former Soviet states who reside in the EU” had been involved in the arson attack.

The SRI also revealed that the group’s activities were not limited to Romania. “Its coordinators in Russia had assigned it a wide range of targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturing facilities, as well as sites of military and industrial interest.”

 

In a separate statement, Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) confirmed that the suspects were a Ukrainian, who was at large in Poland, and two Belarusians, who had already been detained in Germany, where they “had been preparing to commit similar acts”.

Polish broadcaster RMF reports, based on sources, that Artem S.’s role in the Brașov attack was to identify a target and to arrange payment for those involved. A Polish court will now decide whether the 25-year-old should be extradited to Romania.

Poland itself has been a primary target for Russia’s campaign of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” in Europe. Many of those detained and convicted have been Ukrainian and Belarusians, though some Polish citizens have also been implicated.

Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism.

Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026

In some cases, such operatives are amateurs – so-called “disposable agents” – recruited, coordinated and paid through messaging service Telegram. Some have also been pre-existing criminal groups hired by Russia to carry out such tasks.

In August, a drone production plant belonging to private Polish arms company WB Electronics was targeted in an arson attack that Poland has blamed on Russia.

The following month, a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was likewise hit by an arson attack that Poland blamed on Russia. Two Turkish men were later detained in Germany on suspicion of carrying out the attack.

Poland and the United Kingdom have signed the Warsaw Defence Plan, an agreement to enhance their cooperation on security. The aim, says the British Ministry of Defence, is to “deter Russian threats”.

The plan, which follows on from the two countries signing a strategic defence partnership earlier this year, will include joint development and production of defence technologies and military exercises in the Baltic Sea.

The UK and Poland share a deep and historical defence partnership.

Today, Defence Secretary @WesStreeting signed the Warsaw Defence Plan to bring our two nations’ Armed Forces and industries closer together and help ensure collective security in Europe. 🇬🇧🤝🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/IP98D1Qs1L

— Ministry of Defence 🇬🇧 (@DefenceHQ) October 27, 2026

“Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies – from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century,” said British defence secretary Wes Streeting on a visit to Warsaw.

“The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO,” he added.

His Polish counterpart, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, declared that “the Polish-British alliance has never been as strong as it is now”. Both he and Streeting also emphasised the importance of working together to support Ukraine.

 

Among the aims listed for the plan are collaboration in the development and manufacture of next-generation air-defence missiles, as well as drones and counter-drone technologies.

Earlier this year, Poland and the UK, along with Germany, France and Italy, agreed to jointly develop and procure air-defence systems, including missiles and drones.

The Warsaw Defence Plan also pledges to “increase defensive maritime activity in the Baltic Sea through exercises and regional coordination, helping British and Polish forces protect vital lines of communication in the sea”.

The two countries will also seek to build upon existing cooperation between their defence industries, including Poland’s purchase of CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles and 100 launchers from MBDA and last year’s strategic partnership on ammunition production between Poland’s PGZ and Britain’s BAE Systems.

Poland and the UK have signed a major new defence and security treaty.

The agreement includes plans to jointly develop a new air-defence missile, hold large-scale military exercises, and cooperate on countering Russian hybrid attacks https://t.co/cXeYT2u1lw

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026

This week’s agreement builds upon the Northolt Treaty signed by Poland and the UK in May this year, under which the two countries agreed to cooperate more closely on security.

Last year, Poland signed a similar agreement upgrading relations with France. That followed a strategic partnership agreement with Sweden the previous year.

In April this year, Poland signed new comprehensive strategic partnership agreements with South Korea and Japan. This year, it has also deepened security ties with Canada and Norway.

In November, Poland will host the first military exercises organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing. Thousands of personnel from the UK, Poland, France and Germany will test operational readiness for a multinational force to secure a potential future Ukraine peace deal.

]]> US chooses Poland to host service facility for Patriot missiles https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/27/us-chooses-poland-to-host-service-facility-for-patriot-missiles/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:22:13 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106084

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
