The United States has chosen Poland to host a new centre for servicing and maintaining missiles used in Patriot air defence systems, in a decision described as “historic” by both Washington and Warsaw. It was chosen ahead of bids from four other European countries.

The new centre, the first of its kind ot be located outside the US itself, will “dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines”, said the US Department of War, announcing the decision on Tuesday.

Undersecretary of War Michael P. Duffey added that the choice of a country on NATO’s eastern front “sends a clear message [that] the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action”.

Poland Selected to Host Historic PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility, Strengthening Allied Burden-Sharing and Transatlantic Security – U.S. Department of War – Release | @DeptofWar https://t.co/2caqADRRx8

— US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) October 27, 2026

The decision was welcomed by Polish leaders, with defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz saying that it shows “Poland is a trusted ally and holds an extremely important place on the map of global security”.

His deputy minister, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, said that Poland was chosen ahead of rival bids from Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host the facility. However, US ambassador to Poland Thomas Rose indicated that Sweden, not Norway, was the fourth candidate.

Kosiniak-Kamysz and Sobkowiak-Czarnecka both pointed to the role President Karol Nawrocki had played in securing the deal. On many issues, the government is in conflict with the opposition-aligned president, but the two sides worked together on the Patriot bid.

Historyczna decyzja! Centrum serwisowania pocisków PAC-3 do systemów Patriot powstanie w Polsce! 🇵🇱

O europejską lokalizację tej inwestycji rywalizowały cztery państwa, obok Polski – Niemcy, Holandia i Norwegia. Już na etapie składania wniosków polska oferta została oceniona… pic.twitter.com/wUgFhzlzUk

— Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) October 27, 2026

Nawrocki, a conservative, is a close ally of his US counterpart, Donald Trump. The Polish president’s national security advisor, Bartosz Grodecki, claimed that it was “thanks to a conversation between” the two presidents that the new Patriot servicing centre was being established in Poland.

The head of Nawrocki’s foreign policy office, Marcin Przydacz, meanwhile, thanked Washington for choosing Poland to host the new centre.

“The Polish-American alliance and the good atmosphere in relations once again yield results,” he declared. “We can see what positive effects the President’s activity brings for Poland.”

 

Poland is one of a number of European countries that operate Patriot air defence systems. Others include Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Romania, Sweden and Ukraine.

The new centre will service the PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot batteries. The competition to host the facility was announced in July, with the selection made by the US government in conjunction with American defence giant Lockheed Martin, the producer of missiles.

In its press release, the Pentagon emphasised that, although Poland would host the new centre, its work would “be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden”.

Sweden will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine https://t.co/cq9p7OVO7E

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2026

Global demand for Patriot systems has risen significantly, with the United States expending at least 1,500 interceptors in its war with Iran, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Patriot systems have also been crucial in Ukraine’s defence against Russian ballistic missile attacks, although Ukraine’s supply of missiles is now almost entirely exhausted.

After Trump recently suggested that he would authorise Ukraine to produce its own missiles, Poland offered to host any such factory, to ensure its security. However, today’s announcement concerns a site for maintaining and servicing, rather than producing, the missiles.

Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the facility could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security https://t.co/jaQng5wtGg

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 28, 2026

The decision cements Poland’s position as one of Washington’s most important security partners in Europe. War secretary Pete Hegseth has praised Poland as a “model ally”, noting that it has for years met NATO’s defence spending targets, unlike many other member states.

Poland has also been a significant customer for US defence firms. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was NATO’s biggest arms importer, with 44% of the equipment it purchased coming from American suppliers.

Last year, Poland signed a $2 billion deal for the US to provide logistical support and training for Patriot systems. This year, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles.

Poland will become the first country in Europe to produce cruise missiles developed by US defence firm Anduril Industries

The agreement will "transform the continent's defence industry", claims Anduril https://t.co/LPJnwOLfp2

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026

Warsaw is also currently lobbying for a new permanent US military base to be established in Poland, with the government and the president once again putting aside their differences to promote the idea.

Last month, Nawrocki claimed that the proposed base, which he said would be called “Fort Trump”, was “confirmed”. However, Washington has not publicly announced any final decision.

Germany’s economy minister, Katherina Reiche, has praised Poland as an “example of great success”, saying that it offers a model for other countries.

Speaking at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw, which she opened on Monday alongside Polish finance minister Andrzej Domański, Reiche highlighted the deepening trade ties between the two countries.

She noted that bilateral trade last year exceeded €180 billion for the first time, up from €25 billion in 2000, reports Deutsche Welle.

Germany has been Poland’s biggest trading partner for decades, although recent data suggest that China, for the first time in history, overtook Germany as Poland’s largest source of imports in July this year.

Germany has also long been a major investor in Poland. But Reiche welcomed growing recent investments by Polish companies in Germany, which she said was helping to create jobs.

Earlier this year, for example, Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as part of its efforts to expand its operations across Europe.

Reiche noted that around 1,000 Polish companies have invested in Germany, while about 1,600 German companies have invested in Poland, reports Reuters.

Meanwhile, Domański used his remarks at the Polish-German Economic Forum to warn Europe against repeating past mistakes as it confronts a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.

Europe would need a strong economy and new sources of growth to meet those challenges, he added, warning against what he called “economic naivety” and urging Europe – and Germany in particular – not to return to its previous approach to Russia.

The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki.

In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health.

In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases.

 

A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion.

The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%).

The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority).

By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here)

Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now.

No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September.

He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government.

The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border.

However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024

Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision.

The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy.

Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week.

The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland.

 

Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out.

Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves.

Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”.

Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII.

On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024

This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship.

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions.

In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning.

Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago.

Legal scholar @MPiatkowski1 examines the arguments of both sides, explains the legal context, and looks at what could come next https://t.co/xsKAY2TukS

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022

Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland.

If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation.

This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands.

Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute.

Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims

It's time for Germany to fund preservation of the sites, argues @W_Kononczuk https://t.co/08nf4c2jMz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 25, 2026

Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken.

As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful.

But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance.

Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws.

However, the demonstrations, which took place on the sixth anniversary of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) ruling that introduced a near-total abortion ban, were nowhere near the scale of the massive protests that emerged back in 2020.

Było deszczowo, ale nie brakowało ludzi i emocji. Rzeszów pokazał czerwoną kartkę za aborcję rządzącej koalicji. pic.twitter.com/oJo8BiWXxS

— Paweł Preneta (@pawelpreneta) October 22, 2026

In Warsaw, a few hundred people gathered in the rain outside parliament, reported broadcaster RMF. Many held up red cards, a symbol used by the protesters to warn the government that it could be thrown out of power at next year’s parliamentary elections.

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, came to power in December 2023, it pledged to liberalise the abortion laws after eight years of rule by the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party.

In particular, it wanted to reverse the 2020 TK ruling, which outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means abortions can now only take place in two cases: where the pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health.

 

However, in the almost three years since, the government has failed to introduce any new legislation on abortion. One effort to do so in 2024 collapsed amid disagreements between more conservative and liberal elements of Tusk’s coalition.

Finally, earlier this week, the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, approved two abortion bills: one that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling; the other that would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, those measures do not go far enough for many of those attending Tuesday’s protests, who are seeking abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

In any case, both bills approved by the Sejm are likely to be blocked by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of government bills. Nawrocki has made his opposition to abortion clear.

Parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland's abortion laws

One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling that introduced a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise helping women in obtaining unlawful abortions https://t.co/nVj8SQVIsv

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 21, 2026

In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, around 1,000 people attended Thursday’s protest, according to police estimates cited by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Among the placards and banners was one showing Tusk with an extended, Pinocchio-style nose.

“It’s sad that we have to engage in this fight again,” said one of the organisers. “For so long, they ignored us, only coming when they needed votes. Now let’s show that we can’t be ignored.”

In Katowice, around 300 people gathered, according to the Polish Press Agency (PAP). In Poznań, around 400 or so protesters marched to the local headquarters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, where they placed a symbolic red card and waved banners saying “You deceived Poland”.

Czerwona kartka za aborcje. W #Lodz w proteście w strugach deszczu protestuje kilkadziesiąt osób @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/okU7QjnhFw

— Mateusz Szkudlarek (@m_szkudlarek) October 22, 2026

The 2020 TK abortion ruling triggered the largest protests seen in Poland since the communist era, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets. That anger is seen as having played a major role in PiS losing power to Tusk’s coalition in 2023.

Opinion polls consistently show that most Poles want the abortion law to be liberalised, though there remain divisions over whether there should be a return to the pre-2021 status quo or a move even further, to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

In autumn 2027, parliamentary elections will take place, deciding who governs Poland for the next four years. Opinion polls currently show a fairly even split in support between Tusk’s coalition and the right-wing opposition.

Weil, Gotshal and Manges has told its partners the firm should be wound down, in a move that will bring an end to one of the US’s most storied legal firms.

Weil has seen an exodus of partners across the US and London in recent months, including former corporate co-managing partner Michael Hickey and private equity co-head Christopher Machera, who left the firm for US competitor Paul Weiss in August.

Speculation spread across the legal sector in recent months over the future of a firm that was once renowned as a powerhouse in corporate law.

Earlier this month, the New York-headquartered firm was reportedly “negotiating a memorandum of understanding” with an unnamed law firm.

Merger talks fell through

It was understood that the firm in a merger negotiations was its fellow competitor, Willkie Farr & Gallagher, but the talks fell through. 

Bosses of the $2bn ‘white shoe’ firm reportedly told staff to join a company call on Wednesday afternoon, where they were informed the company was set to be dissolved, the Financial Times reported.

A Weil spokesperson said in a statement: “For more than 90 years, Weil, Gotshal & Manges has had the privilege of advising clients on some of their most consequential matters.

“Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm’s Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down.

“The partners are expected to vote in the coming days. During the wind-down process over the coming months, the Firm will continue serving clients with the dedication and excellence that have defined it since its founding and will remain committed to supporting its colleagues,” they added.

The 95-year-old law firm has over 2,000 staff worldwide. The firm has had an office in London since 1996, where the headcount sits around the 400 mark.

John Bringardner, head of financial analytics firm Debtwire, said following the failed merger talks, there was a crisis of confidence among Weil’s top partners.

“Ultimately, it is this crisis of confidence that has caused the liquidation, rather than the debt or overspending seen in other large firm collapses, such as Dewey & LeBoeuf,” he said 

Bringardner added, “The firm itself will enter wind-down mode and may file for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in an attempt to reject its office leases, while lawyers, staff, and clients will be free to move to other firms.“

Culture writer Adam Bloodworth tried to watch the Budget 2026 in full. Here’s how that went, with all the excruciating detail

I am an alien in the City AM office. While the other journalists concern themselves with taxation and business rates, I am writing about theatre and restaurants. City AM’s tagline is ‘business with personality,’ and, humblebrag alert, I suppose I’m the personality. 

By and large, politics and business is left off our pages – we like to take the reader away from their desks to somewhere more fabulous. And while important conversations take place over dinner, we’re concerned with telling you what to eat, where to go, and, crucially, who to put on the invite list. 

And so it was new for me this year to sit through the entirety of the Budget – not just have it on in the background, but properly take it in. Here’s this lifestyle writer’s takeaways from the Autumn Budget 2026.

Call me a fish out of water, flailing desperately for validation in City AM’s hallowed towers.

Budget 2026: I started with giant ambitions

I can take all this in. I can definitely take all this in. It’s basically an hour off work: watching a man deliver a speech about how he’s going to change the country. I’m sure my parents must have sat down, like millions of others around the country, as a form of national service, to listen intently to this twice-annual sermon, only for the viewing experience to turn sour after about four-and-a-half minutes, when I had my first intrusive thought about pizza. All my hopes are quickly dashed. My mind wandering has caused me to lose the flow, and I’ve mucked this up, already. I thought I’d have at least 12 minutes in me. I can’t believe how quickly this has happened.

This isn’t going to work

This is too much information. Like, if ten minutes of someone talking fairly quickly without pausing feels like a lot of information, this is more than six times that. I really like Louis Theroux, but when I saw him say some fascinating things at How The Light Gets In festival this summer, I found myself thinking about pizza again. Sixty minutes is a long time. This is hopeless.

New approach

“You learn which bits to focus on!” my journo friend hollers from across the desk, shifting his headphones when he notices me in trouble. I can tell he’s half-zoned-out too, as he noticed me in the first place. This sounds good, and it kind of works. I tune in and have some Budget 2026 takeaways, like how “half of our shops, restaurants and gyms will pay no business rates at all”, but at other times it is still hopeless. By the time I’ve tuned back into the discourse, the Chancellor has sped ahead and moved onto something else. I feel useless, and dumb, like a stupid dumb baby. 

Maybe that’s enough?

But I did learn something. I learned about founders’ relief and first time buyer ISAs and how we’re going to get 4p off gherkins, which loyal readers will know I’m very excited about. I did learn something. A lot, actually. Now I can relay this new skill to other life situations when friends bore me to tears tell me about their lives.

The pantomime stuff is so dumb

I know I’m the gazillionth person to say this, but how are ordinary people supposed to relate to the Budget 2026, and politics in general, when everyone in the Commons is literally making noises like a cow? Not to mention all the pointing and jeering, and making sassy comments. Deputy speaker Nursat Ghani told MPs they were behaving like their children, but she wasn’t much better, clapping back at one MP’s Budget rebuttal by telling him he’d “have to write yourself a prescription just to calm down”. It was one of a handful of panto villain remarks. She told another talkative MP: “I think you’ve spoken more words than the Chancellor during this statement.” It’s funny in the sense that Ghani has good comic timing, but tragic in that this Budget is affecting people’s lives and it seems like making cow noises and cracking jokes takes precedence over the politics.

The Budget 2026 is published online anyway

Don’t sweat it: everything’s published online, on the government website, minutes after the Budget 2026 speech is delivered in the Commons. So you can sit down and read it like a slow, wise old tortoise. I’d insert something here about how that’s what happens in politics anyway – everything takes forever and no one gets anything done, etcetera etcetera – but that would require me having taken in more of the Budget than I did, so I’ll just end this here. My head hurts.

The Chancellor has set up a new defence financing taskforce and unveiled fresh funding for investment in the arms industry amid a concerted effort to lean on the private sector to drive Britain’s rearmament push.

John Healey swerved any concrete public sector defence pledges at his maiden Budget, promising to provide detail on how the government will meet its pledges at next year’s spending review.

Instead, the Yorkshire MP unveiled a flurry of measures to help boost investment in the UK’s defence industry, which would be spearheaded by a new ‘Innovative Defence Financing Taskforce’, he said.

Healey told MPs he was “determined to use more innovative financing, alongside the private sector and our international allies” amid the government’s drive to boost its defence capabilities.

Comulytic Note Pro | ★★★★☆ | £128 (plus optional subscriptions)

Every journalist has had that dreaded moment: you leave an interview, click play on the recorder – or, more likely, tap your phone – and… nothing. The worst silence in the world. The interview didn’t record.

Over a couple of decades in the game, this has happened to me a handful of times but none worse than the time I interviewed a proper A-lister, a man once tipped to play Bond, only to discover something went wrong with the recording. Just 40 minutes of low, unusable crackle. I remember sitting on the kerb desperately trying to write down everything he’d said so I wouldn’t have to break it to my editor that I’d screwed the pooch. To this day I now always bring two recording devices to big interviews, usually my phone and my trusty – but massive – iPad Pro.

So when I saw the new wave of dinky little AI transcription devices, I was keen to take one for a spin.

The Comulytic Note Pro AI voice recorder review

Enter the Comulytic Note Pro, which is one of my favourite gadgets of the year. The first thing you notice about this little recorder is its size. It’s the rough dimensions of three stacked credit cards, and weighs about the same. 

It’s crafted from brushed aluminium – de rigueur in new tech since Apple started using it in the early 2000s – with a tiny little LED screen, a play/pause/record button and not a whole bunch else. Mine comes in a shade Comulytic will not be allowed to call Cosmic Orange but is clearly designed to complement the iPhone 17 Pro, about whose colour I positively gushed this time last year.

It’s also supplied with a neat little black wallet that snaps to the back of your iPhone. I’m sold: but what does it actually do?

Well, pair it with your phone through the companion app, hit the record button (a two second press) and it starts taping your conversations. It then automatically – and immediately – syncs the conversation to the app, where you then have a few options.

As I’m using it for journalism – mostly recording one-on-one conversations – I have mostly been using the basic, free tier, which uses AI to generate a transcript of your conversations. It works about as well as any transcription software I’ve tried – Otter has been my go-to but I didn’t notice a big drop-off in quality with the Note Pro. And, as I need to store all my recordings in case someone tries to sue me, I was pleased with how easy it is to export both the written transcripts and the audio files.

Advancer options include translation

More advanced options include the ability to translate what people are saying into other languages (113 of them, including Sudanese and Malay), although for that you’ll have to subscribe to the premium tier (£10 a month), which comes with unlimited translation and “insights” into your audio recordings. There’s also an Elite tier (£29.99 a month), which offers an additional AI agent who can access your emails and create slides and documents.

The paid tiers can also analyse your transcripts and offer insights and action points, which would probably be useful if you were using your Note Pro for meetings rather than interviews. But the fact you can get unlimited free transcription is perfect for me, especially when most of Comulytic’s rivals cap the number of free minutes you get per month (although the inability to turn off the links asking for money is a little annoying).

The battery is supposedly good for 45 hours of continuous recording – after trialling it for a few weeks, I’m still sitting on two bars. 

And… there’s not much else to say, really. I came to the Note Pro looking for a second recording device and what I got was… a second recording device, albeit one with more AI bells and whistles than I will ever use. And at £128, it falls nicely into the “treat yourself” category – a nice little present that won’t tip you into the red.

The Comulytic Action Pro

I also tried out the more expensive and more capable Comulytic Action Pro, which does everything the Note Pro does but is even more skewed towards being an all-encompassing digital assistant, specialising in turning your transcripts into slideshows or emails or… whatever you like, really.

It has six microphones compared to the Note’s two and its battery lasts for 70 hours. It also has a built-in magnet, so it can clip firmly to your phone without a wallet. But it’s not made from orange brushed aluminium and it’s not the size of a stack of credit cards and if I had to choose one, I’d pick the entry level Note Pro every time.

In his maiden Budget today, the Chancellor also revealed fresh measures to tackle the risks posed by autonomous technology, including a National Agentic Security Unit tasked with detecting and responding to AI systems operating outside their intended controls.

Healey told MPs that “nowhere is the necessary role for the state clearer than in AI”, pledging an approach built on security and sovereignty.

The Treasury said AI could add between 0.4 and 1.3 percentage points to annual UK productivity growth over the next decade, citing OECD estimates, but warned that the technology also posed risks to online safety and national security.

The new £40m unit will develop capabilities to monitor rogue AI agents and respond to incidents, as businesses and public services increasingly deploy systems capable of acting autonomously.

A further £70m will establish a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre to identify weaknesses across critical infrastructure, while £60m will fund a National Cyber Shield using AI to strengthen Britain’s cyber defences.

The government also committed £24m to improving cyber security across public services, including hospitals, schools and local authorities.

Ministers will consult next year on where liability for cyber breaches should fall and how to tackle insecure technology at source.

The Chancellor was right to acknowledge the contribution financial and related professional services make to jobs and investment across the UK. But his measures didn’t consistently match that ambition. A ‘do no harm’ Budget was our test. It is one that the Chancellor has not quite met. While the increase in the bank tax surcharge from January next year from three per cent to six per cent is specifically timebound to 15 months, its impact nevertheless hits the UK’s attractiveness compared to its main competitors. Tax decisions affecting this industry have consequences across the country.

For businesses looking to start, expand or invest, access to finance is key. The economic test is whether policy decisions make that easier or harder to secure. Any constraint on the capacity for firms across our industry to finance businesses risks working against the government’s ambition to increase investment.

Capital, businesses and talent are increasingly mobile. Raising revenue today must not come at the expense of the investment that supports the UK’s future growth and status as a world-class international financial centre.

The Chancellor’s decision not to remove Stamp Duty on UK equities was a missed opportunity to lower investment costs and strengthen UK capital markets. Encouraging companies to raise capital, grow and remain in the UK requires the right investment environment. Leaving this unnecessary barrier in place does not advance that ambition. As expected, John Healey delivered a low-key ‘first do no harm’ Budget, with a few treats for households and businesses and no nasty surprises for investors. What was needed, though, was a ‘do some real good’ Budget.

The only ‘rabbit’ was a £100 ‘household energy payment’ for 20m households in council tax bands A–D, costing £2.6bn. But even this merely replaced a widely trailed expansion of the Warm Home Discount.

The Chancellor had already ruled out many of the dafter ideas favoured by his colleagues, including equalising capital gains and income tax, or a new wealth tax. Despite their simplistic appeal, the Treasury and Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) will have told him that neither idea would raise much money.

Two brave decisions

Two decisions were still ‘brave’. The first was to cut fiscal headroom from about £24bn to £15bn in 2029-30, rebuilding it only partially to £22bn in 2030-31.

Healey gambled that markets would accept this as a sensible way to avoid further growth-damaging tax rises in response to what may only be temporary energy shock. What is the point of an emergency buffer if you do not use it?

So far, this gamble seems to have paid off: bond yields barely moved, though UK government borrowing costs remain the highest in the G7.

Tax rises of around £6bn in 2029-30 were also much smaller than feared, and about a tenth of those announced by Healey’s predecessor.

The second brave decision risked angering Labour activists by slowing the increases in the national minimum wage for younger workers. However, there is ample evidence that large minimum wage hikes have reduced job opportunities, especially in retail and hospitality.

For the City, the main news was the increase in the bank surcharge on corporation tax. But at three percentage points for just 15 months, it was smaller than feared, and major banks’ shares rallied slightly.

Healey also confirmed £15.4bn in additional funding for the National Wealth Fund and £5bn for the British Business Bank, two Public Financial Institutions, or ‘PuFIns’.

Some call this ‘off balance sheet’ funding, or even ‘fiddling the books’, because borrowing offset by acquiring a financial asset is neutral for the targeted debt measure, PSNFL.

That criticism seems unfair: these activities remain transparently on the balance sheet.

But there is a broader concern that more borrowing is still more borrowing, whatever its purpose, and the state’s record of investing your money wisely is dismal.

A Ming Vase Budget

Overall, this was a ‘Ming Vase Budget’. Healey has tried to avoid breaking anything – including Labour’s poll lead – in what may be the last major fiscal event before Burnham calls an early election.

Crucially, most of Burnham’s big ideas will require a new mandate. Some carry a hefty price tag, including a much larger role for the state in providing social care, infrastructure, utilities and housing, while others would cross existing manifesto red lines, notably by seeking a much closer relationship with the EU.

In contrast, a ‘do some real good’ Budget would have rolled back the increases in taxes and regulations that have raised UK business costs, starting with employers’ NI and the Employment Rights Act.

It would also abolish the most damaging taxes, notably stamp duty on property and shares, or at least simplify and improve the tax system in revenue-neutral ways.

We also need a credible medium- to long-term plan to control public spending, requiring tough decisions on the state’s size and role.

Unfortunately, these decisions will probably have to wait until the next parliament, and possibly for a different government.

Julian Jessop is an independent economist

The Chancellor has allocated an extra £20.4bn to the country’s two major state-owned policy banks for the next five-years. The National Wealth Fund will get around £15.4bn, while the British Business Bank will receive £5bn.

“I will work with pension providers, asset managers and the wider industry to accelerate more private investment into Britain’s innovative, fast-growth firms,” the Chancellor said.

Later in his speech, Healey confirmed the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank would “launch a new focus on defence, dual use technology and sovereign capability, deploying up to £5bn of investment and lending over the next four years”.

While not a direct breach of the fiscal rules, the government’s use of public finance bodies (Pufins) to borrow more cash has become a lightning rod for criticism.

Oxford Economics said in August the move would be “an accounting trick to raise investment within the fiscal rules. But it would increase the government’s financing needs and risks undermining its fiscal credibility.”

Healey takes advantage of Reeves’ rule change

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves changed the fiscal rules in her first Budget in October 2024, switching the government’s headline debt target from public sector net debt to public sector net financial liabilities (PSNFL).

Under the new system, financial assets count against debt, so when the Treasury funds a Pufin to make a loan or buy an equity stake, the asset it acquires offsets the borrowing. This paves the way for the government to channel more money into investment through Pufins without raising the measured debt figure.

But the fiscal watchdog has previously warned about such moves, writing in its 2025 fiscal risks report that the borrowing mechanism could have unintended side effects.

They added politicians would be “incentivised to use financing mechanisms such as loans and equity to meet a given policy objective, even if this is not the best value for money mechanism”.

Healey’s manoeuvre comes as pressure mounts to meet the target of spending three per cent of GDP on defence by 2030. Healey resigned as defence secretary under Sir Keir Starmer after the government failed to commit sufficient funding to the armed forces and demanded a timetable to meet the three per cent target.

Harry Kane wore the legendary Rolex Daytona at the Ballon d’Or ceremony – but not the right one

In 1979, when Trevor Francis became Britain’s first-ever million-pound football player, it generated headlines around the world. The British press and parliament treated it like a moral crisis. Could anyone really be worth seven figures? Today, a player can wear that amount on his wrist and it barely causes a ripple on the gossip pages.

Today, the question is whether a watch can really be worth seven figures. If you were to ask me whether, in a perfect world, I would blow over a million quid on a Rolex Oyster Perpetual Cosmograph “Blue Sapphire” Daytona: Ref. 126599TSA, as worn by Harry Kane when he accepted his Ballon d’Or, I’d have to say ‘no’.

Which is odd, because I love Rolex Daytonas. I have, on occasion, considered swapping one of my kidneys for a 1964 Rolex Daytona Ref: 6239. It’s a truly sexy beast, where Harry’s timepiece is more Ray Winstone in his golden “budgie smugglers” in the film of that name.

The original Rolex Daytona

The original Ref: 6239 was a lean, mean stainless steel tool watch, designed following the mantra of the 3Fs: form follows function. Its design was driven by the needs and wants of racing drivers. This was a watch with a purpose, and that purpose was speed and the timing thereof. It allowed wearers to measure elapsed time and calculate average speed. It’s even named after the historic home of US motor racing, Daytona Beach, and was worn by real racing drivers and pit crews. The fact it is one of the most beautiful watches ever made was almost an accident.

The only part of that rich heritage shared with the watch Harry Kane wore at the London Palladium is the name. This incarnation is cast in white gold, with 36 baguette-cut blue sapphires around the bezel and 54 diamonds on the case and lugs, with even more sapphires on the dial as hour markers.

The dial itself is made of obsidian, a volcanic glass that, while it reflects light beautifully, is a nightmare to machine into a functioning dial. I’m not sure it’s worth the effort. While its official factory configuration is the ref. 126599TSA, released last year, this is an off-catalogue version.

You see, the world has changed since 1979, when almost anyone could pick up a Daytona. Nowadays, it’s a status symbol, the ultimate statement that you have arrived. It is one of those things that vulgar money alone is not supposed to be able to buy; the currency that counts here is not fortune but fame, and the more famous the better.

Other dazzling watches at sporting events

It exists in the same rarefied world as the flashy Rolex Daytona “Rainbow” worn by Spanish tennis star Carlos Alcaraz at the 2026 World Cup Final. It’s also a sibling of the $1m blinged-up Rolex Daytona “Blue Sapphire” worn by Roger Federer at the 2025 Laver Cup (a watch that, judging by his expression, was much admired by Alcaraz).

To get one of these off-catalogue watches, you need to be the right kind of celebrity, and either a Rolex ambassador or a serious friend of the brand. And rich. Very rich.

I don’t have a problem with any of that. It’s your money, spend it how you want. As to whether any watch can be worth a million quid, I can think of plenty that probably are. 

My only problem with Harry’s Rolex is the name. It’s a bit like me changing my name to Margo, putting on a diamond-encrusted tutu, and expecting to be able to plié. To me, the Daytona is sacred: save the sapphires and diamonds for another model.

• Andy is Picture Editor at City AM

Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:13:59 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Researchers tracked the passwords 154 people used online for an average of 147 days and found them logging into 26 websites with fewer than 10 unique passwords — roughly 60 percent were reused outright or built from pieces of passwords they were already using elsewhere https://siliconcanals.com/d-researchers-tracked-the-passwords-154-people-used-online-for-an-average-of-147-days-and-found-them-logging-into-26-websites-with-fewer-than-10-unique-passwords-roughly-60-percent-were-reused/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:30:40 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109740

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

]]> At 19, an Estonian borrowed €5,000 from his family and recruited Tallinn taxi drivers face-to-face for an app he had built because the city’s taxis were unreliable; twelve years later the company took €2.27 billion in revenue in more than 50 countries and posted its first annual profit — €920,000, a margin of four hundredths of one percent https://siliconcanals.com/n-at-19-an-estonian-borrowed-e5000-from-his-family-and-recruited-tallinn-taxi-drivers-face-to-face-for-an-app-he-had-built-because-the-citys-taxis-were-unreliable-twelve-years-later-the-company-took/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:00:26 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109712

An Estonian founder’s company posted its first annual net profit in 2025: €920,000 on €2.27 billion in revenue.]]>

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

A decade of growth without a profit

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Who was willing to fund a decade of losses

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Bolt said at the time the money would go toward opening more of the small, city-centre “dark stores” that supply its 15-minute grocery delivery service, and toward pushing further into new geographic markets, the same expansion strategy that had defined the company since Villig first stood on a Tallinn street corner recruiting drivers by hand. That January 2022 round is the most recent outside capital the company has raised at scale; the 2025 results suggest it hasn’t needed another one since.

The first profit, and how thin it was

That changed with the 2025 financial year. According to Bolt’s own results, reported in coverage from Trade with Estonia, the company took €2.27 billion in revenue across more than 50 countries, a 14 percent increase on the year before, and posted its first-ever annual net profit: €920,000. Set against €2.27 billion in revenue, that works out to a margin of roughly four hundredths of one percent, the kind of number that is technically profitable and not much more. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. Villig described the underlying business as having reached a $14 billion gross merchandise value run-rate with two consecutive years of positive cash flow, arguably the more meaningful signal for a company at Bolt’s stage than the net income line itself.

What a four-hundredths-of-a-percent margin actually means

A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. The accounts do not reveal whether Bolt targeted that result or whether it could sustain growth without further external financing. They show a small net profit and positive operating cash flow for the year, not permanent financial independence. It hasn’t settled every question that scale raises, either.

In November 2024, a UK employment tribunal ruled that Bolt’s drivers qualify as workers rather than independent contractors — a ruling on status only, with compensation still to be set at a separate hearing. Leigh Day, the law firm representing roughly 15,000 drivers in the claim, estimates the compensation owed could exceed £200 million, or upwards of £15,000 per driver on average, according to Leigh Day’s own statement. Whether a margin this thin holds, thickens, or gets eaten by exactly that kind of regulatory ruling as Bolt pushes into new cities, verticals and eventually autonomous vehicles is the open question its 2025 results don’t settle either way.

]]> A country of fewer than 1.4 million people has produced ten billion-dollar startups — about 7 for every million residents, more than three times the US rate — and the first of them was a voice-call app a handful of engineers built in Tallinn in 2003. https://siliconcanals.com/n-a-country-of-fewer-than-1-4-million-people-has-produced-ten-billion-dollar-startups-about-7-for-every-million-residents-more-than-three-times-the-us-rate/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 10:00:24 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109711

Estonia ranks second in the cited per-capita tally—and first in the EU—with about 7.1 startups that have reached a billion-dollar valuation per million residents.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: The original excerpt called Estonia the world leader, although the cited per-capita tally places it second behind Liechtenstein. The article also misstated the Tiger Leap school-internet rollout; first-party history says all schools were connected by 2001.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

That per-capita figure is a calculation built on CB Insights’ data, not a ranking CB Insights itself publishes, and it is worth reading as a proxy for the ecosystem’s density rather than a formal league table.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The one that started it

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Its founders, the Swede Niklas Zennström and the Dane Janus Friis, co-founded the company with three Estonian engineers, Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn, who built the software behind what was then an unusually good way to make free voice calls over the internet. eBay bought the company two years later for a reported $2.6 billion in upfront cash and stock (total consideration including later earn-outs was reported as high as $4.1 billion).

Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

Why the count kept growing

The clearest example of that inheritance is Wise. Its co-founder Taavet Hinrikus was Skype’s first employee; his eventual co-founder, Kristo Käärmann, worked at Deloitte in London. Both were Estonians living abroad with an ordinary, irritating problem: Hinrikus was paid in euros but lived in the UK, and Käärmann was paid in pounds but had a mortgage back in Estonia in euros. According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. They launched TransferWise, later renamed Wise, in 2011, and it went public in London a decade later, making both founders Estonia’s first tech billionaires.

That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Milda Mitkutė was changing apartments in Vilnius in 2008 and had more clothes than the new place could hold. Rather than throw them out, she wanted a way to pass them on to people she knew. The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. Underneath the fee structure sits a harder problem: getting a stranger’s old jumper from a seller’s flat to a buyer’s front door, cheaply and reliably, across dozens of countries.
