An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

I used to think of a certain kind of person as a weather system. You know the type. You ask how the traffic was and somehow you have insulted their driving, their neighbourhood and their late mother. Everything lands as a slight. Everything requires a correction.

For years my take on this was simple and a bit smug. Attention seekers. People who enjoy the theatre of being wronged.

Then I started reading the actual psychology, and it turns out I had the story backwards. The people who seem offended by everything are rarely shopping for a fight. Most of them are running a security detail, and they have been running it since they were small.

When insults were the weather, everything looks like an insult

Here is the mechanism. If you grow up somewhere that regularly treats you as a target, your brain gets very good at spotting incoming fire. That is not a flaw. In the original environment it was survival. The problem is that the skill does not switch off when you move somewhere safer.

Psychologists call this hostile attribution bias, and it shows up early. Researchers followed around 1,300 children across nine countries and gave them scenarios where someone’s behaviour could be read as an accident or as deliberate. A shove in a corridor. A joke that could go either way. The children who consistently read hostile intent went on to show higher rates of persistent aggressive behaviour, even after accounting for how aggressive they had already been.

Two children see the same shove. One files it under accident, one files it under attack. Twenty years later, one of them is the adult who somehow takes offence at the weather report.

Being told you are too much is its own training

The other route in is quieter and I suspect more common.

Some people are not knocked around. They are simply corrected, constantly, about their own inner life. You are not upset. You are not tired. That did not hurt. Stop being dramatic. Clinicians call this an invalidating environment, a setting that consistently dismisses or punishes someone for expressing what they feel or need.

The theory behind that term was built to explain a specific clinical picture, so I would not go throwing it at your touchy colleague as a diagnosis. But the underlying logic travels. If your read on your own experience gets overruled a thousand times, you learn something ugly. You learn that your sense of things will not be taken seriously unless you make it loud.

And making it loud is exactly what the rest of us punish. We call it oversensitivity. We are reading the receipt and ignoring the purchase.

The tax the sensitive person pays

None of this is a free pass, and here is where it stops being sympathetic.

Researchers describe a disposition they call rejection sensitivity, meaning a tendency to anxiously expect rejection, spot it readily, and react hard when you think you have found it. People high in it tend to be less satisfied in their close relationships, and their partners report the same.

The trap is that the vigilance manufactures the thing it fears. You brace for the cold shoulder, so you go cold first. Your partner feels the chill and pulls back. Now you have evidence. Now the system that was built to protect your dignity has quietly started demolishing it.

I have watched this happen up close, over what I promise you was a genuinely neutral text message. There was no villain in that story. There was a very old alarm and a very ordinary Tuesday.

What actually helps when you are on the receiving end

Arguing about whether the offence was reasonable is a losing game. The alarm is not calibrated to this conversation. It was calibrated years ago, by somebody else.

Try naming the feeling without conceding the facts. Something like: I can see that landed badly, and I did not mean it that way. That costs you nothing on the question of intent, and it grants them something rare, which is agreement that their reaction was real. It does more work than an hour of you proving your innocence.

Be boringly consistent. Vigilance responds to evidence, not reassurance, and that takes months. You cannot talk someone out of a threat detector. You can only give it a long run of days where nothing bad happens.

And hold your line anyway. Understanding why someone snaps is not the same as accepting being snapped at. You can say plainly that you will not be shouted at and still mean everything above.

And if the thin skin is yours

Then start somewhere other than whether you were right. You often are. Slights are real, and some of the people telling you to calm down are exactly the ones worth watching.

The more useful question is what the alertness is costing you. Running security is expensive. It eats your Sundays. It makes you rehearse conversations that never happen and re-read messages for tone that was never there. My grandmother had a version of this. It made her formidable company. I think it also made her lonely.

So build a delay. When something lands wrong, wait a day before you respond. Graciousness has nothing to do with it. You are checking whether the feeling survives a night’s sleep. Usually it does not. The ones that do are worth taking seriously, and now you can take them seriously without the static.

]]>

The post North American robot orders climb 24.8% in Q3 of 2026, says A3 appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

While automotive OEM orders declined in the first half of 2026, they picked up in Q3. Source: A3

North American companies ordered 10,989 robots valued at $723.5 million in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest data from the Association for Advancing Automation, or A3. Orders increased 24.8% in units and 26.1% in value compared with the third quarter of 2025, making it the strongest quarter of the year so far, it said.

The third-quarter gains pushed total orders for the first nine months of 2026 to 28,984 robots valued at approximately $1.89 billion, A3 reported. This represented increases of 9.6% in units and 13.3% in value over the same period last year, noted the Ann Arbor, Mich.-based organization.

Orders grow in automotive in addition to other industries

After declining during the first half of 2026, automotive OEM robot orders returned to positive year-over-year growth in the third quarter, increasing 7.5%, said A3. Orders from automotive component suppliers climbed 90.4%, continuing the strong demand from that segment seen earlier in the year.

Several other industries recorded substantial increases in robot orders during Q3:

  • Semiconductors and electronics/photonics: +97.6% units
  • Plastics and rubber: +67.7% units
  • Life sciences/pharmaceutical/biomedical: +38.7% units
  • Metals: +37.0% units

All other industries increased just 0.5% in units ordered, while food and consumer goods declined by 23.7%, A3 added.

The growth in the electronics segment occurred as investment grew in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, with strong demand for electronics supporting AI and other applications. Life sciences has also seen continued investment in domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing among others, said A3.

Automotive component orders were particularly strong despite earlier weakness among automotive manufacturing, said the organization. While OEM orders improved in Q3, they remained 17% below their year-earlier level through the first nine months of 2026.

“What stands out in the third quarter is not simply the magnitude of the growth, but how broadly it was distributed across the market,” stated Alex Shikany, executive vice president at A3. “Automotive OEM orders returned to positive growth, while automotive components and sectors such as semiconductors/electronics and life sciences posted significant gains. That broader mix is important because it points to a robotics market that is becoming increasingly diversified across industries and applications.”

Submit your innovation now!

Cobot orders increase 56%, finds A3

Force- and power-limited or collaborative robots also posted a strong third quarter, with 1,831 units valued at $63.8 million ordered. This was an increase of about 56% in units compared with Q3 2025. Collaborative robots accounted for 16.7% of all robot units ordered during the quarter.

Through September, North American companies ordered 4,605 cobots valued at approximately $178 million, representing 15.9% of total robot units and 9.4% of order value.

Collaborative robots continue to be used across a wide range of applications and industries. In the first nine months of 2026, cobots accounted for 43.8% of robot orders in life sciences/pharma/biomed and 36.9% in semi & electronics/photonics.

Manufacturing activity continues expansion

The stronger robot order numbers come alongside improving manufacturing activity, said A3. The September Institute of Supply Chain Management (ISM) Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) registered 54.5, marking a ninth consecutive month of expansion, while the Federal Reserve said that U.S. manufacturing output increasing 0.3% in September.

Higher input costs, trade uncertainty, and the timing of large manufacturing projects remain factors to watch, noted A3. “But with robot orders strengthening across several industries, the North American market enters the final quarter of 2026 with positive momentum,” it said.

More detailed Q3 2026 market data and graphs are available upon request for press and through the A3 Vault for member companies. A3 said it is the leading global advocate for the benefits of automating.

A3 has also expanded its Market Intelligence resources with “Business of Automation,” a weekly show examining industry developments; Business of Automation on Substack, offering additional analysis and industry updates; and SIGNAL, a free research series covering robotics, automation, and AI.

Association members seeking deeper insights can subscribe to MI+ for forecasts, detailed datasets, dashboards and industry analysis. A3 members represent more than 1,500 manufacturers, component suppliers, system integrators, end users, academic institutions, research groups, and consulting firms.

The post What Symbotic’s Walmart growth teaches robotics startups about anchor customers appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Symbotic’s recent quarterly filing lists its largest customer, together with affiliates, as “Customer A,” and the annual report names that customer as Walmart. Customer A supplied 90.5% of revenue in the quarter that ended June 27, 2026. Symbotic reported $720.8 million in revenue and $55 million in net income for the same quarter.

Few robotics companies have turned one demanding customer into a business this size, and this profit follows earlier profits. The quarter also included $19.4 million of investment gains and negative non-GAAP free cash flow, so one quarter’s profit can’t settle whether leaning so heavily on Walmart has paid off.

For a startup founder deciding whether to sign a second customer soon, Walmart’s 90.5% share says little about the cost of serving another account. I’d look at how many people that account pulls into the field and what the contract obliges each side to do when plans change. I’d also ask how easily the anchor could get the same work done another way.

Walmart wrote its own insurance

Symbotic can’t afford to lose Walmart, and that dependence already gives the retailer some protection. Walmart’s contracts show that it didn’t rely on that incentive alone. The 2022 master automation agreement gives Walmart continuity rights, including the right to embed engineers with Symbotic and technical material held in escrow, which Walmart can use under specified conditions. The 2025 agreement for Walmart’s store-level Accelerated Pickup and Delivery (APD) systems repeats those protections. During the APD build-out, it also caps, at a redacted number, how many comparable APD systems Symbotic can sell to each outside customer every year. The filings don’t show whether Walmart has ever tested these rights, so they read more like preparation than a proven fallback.

When the APD deal closed in January 2025, Walmart committed $520 million of development funding. Symbotic paid Walmart a $200 million base price for its robotics business in the same transaction and agreed to two possible milestone payments of $175 million each. Symbotic gained funded development and the prospect of a large rollout, although the additional purchase commitment depends on performance milestones. In return, it accepted delivery obligations and limits on comparable APD sales to other customers.

Every new site borrows people

Operations-heavy robotics companies tend to add people as they add customers, at least until deployment becomes routine. Symbotic reported about 2,000 employees at the end of fiscal 2025, with roughly half working at customer sites to install, commission, and maintain its systems, and it brings in contractors as needed. Its standard model also has Symbotic operate a new system for a limited time before handing daily operation to the customer. Those field teams serve both new deployments and running systems, so the total can’t show what one more site would take. It does show how much of the business still happens where the robots are installed.

Where the newer Symbotic demand comes from

Symbotic has broadened its customer base, partly through structures it helped build. Exol, its warehouse-as-a-service venture with SoftBank, accounted for $11.6 billion of the $22.5 billion backlog at June 27, 2026, and Symbotic owns 35% of Exol and helps fund its build-out. Walmart de México, another newer customer, is majority-owned by Walmart. Exol lets customers use Symbotic’s system without buying it outright, and Walmex carries a proven relationship into a new market, so both routes make commercial sense. Both also move partly with decisions made by Symbotic or Walmart, so the longer customer list carries somewhat less independent demand than its length suggests.

Submit your innovation now!

A new Symbotic customer can take two years to go live

Symbotic’s management said in 2023 that it aimed to add one or two new customers a year. It has also described its historical timeline as about 24 months from a signed statement of work to acceptance. Medline signed in late fiscal 2025 and plans a pilot in 2027. Associated Wholesale Grocers announced a project in March 2026 and expects operations in the fourth quarter of 2027. Associated Food Stores announced its agreement in May 2023 and had its first phase running by February 2025.

Symbotic generally recognizes system revenue as it incurs costs, once acceptance is reasonably assured, so revenue can start before installation and well before go-live. The 24-month timeline instead shows how long a supplier can wait before a new customer’s site actually runs, which is when it learns whether the product traveled.

What I expect and what would change my mind

The scenario I would examine most closely has no villain. Walmart stays satisfied, meets its commitments, and finishes the distribution-center rollout on schedule. System revenue from that program then winds down, and the work that continues, mostly service and software, brings in less than installation did unless new system orders follow. The supplier did everything right, and its growth now depends on replacing a program that ended as planned. For Symbotic, the APD program and Exol are the obvious candidates to replace it, along with newer accounts, and I would watch whether they reach real scale before the distribution-center work tapers.

I expect Walmart to remain Symbotic’s dominant customer for years, and I’d be surprised to see its share fall below 80% before fiscal 2028. Walmart keeps expanding its own commitments, with the performance-dependent APD program added on top of the distribution-center rollout. New accounts tend to start with one site or a pilot, and management’s stated aim in 2023 was one or two new customers a year. Even with revenue recognized as costs are incurred, a single new site adds little next to dozens of Walmart projects moving at once. Exol is my largest uncertainty. Its revenue counts outside Walmart, so a faster build-out of its contracted systems could pull down Walmart’s reported share, even though I would still treat Exol separately when judging independent demand. A faster Exol ramp, or larger near-term rollouts by unrelated customers, would change my view.

I also expect strategic buyers to lean harder on contractual control. Protective terms of this kind already appear in automation contracts. I think buyers who invest in warehouse and humanoid startups, or deploy their robots at scale, will ask for them more often and in broader forms.

The same field-load logic explains why I expect a shakeout among humanoid pilots over the next few years. A pilot at one site with a few robots can run on subsidy. The robot maker’s engineers can install the robots, step in when one stalls, and absorb support costs that the pilot price doesn’t recover. A fleet contract tends to turn those hidden costs into obligations. When the buyer pays a fixed service price for uptime, extra interventions come out of the vendor’s margin. The humanoid companies that reach paid fleets will probably be the ones that used their pilots to measure and cut the field work each robot needs. A famous customer or a large funding round won’t guarantee that step. If several of these companies grow paid fleets and keep support costs predictable, I’d expect a milder shakeout than I do now.

What startups can take from Symbotic

Walmart got continuity rights and limits on Symbotic’s comparable sales in exchange for funding and scale. I think founders tend to judge an anchor deal by the size of the order and skim terms like these. A better habit is to go through the contract clause by clause and ask what each restriction costs in buyers the company can no longer pursue. The money deserves the same scrutiny, since every dollar comes with something to deliver or repay.

That funding goes furthest when it buys repeatability. Symbotic’s management has described moving testing to suppliers and standardizing build and test procedures, work that can pay off on every later deployment.

Startups do the same fieldwork with far fewer people. A second customer on the same system still pulls staff into the field, and one that needs a different integration pulls more of them, usually off the anchor’s rollout. Because the same small team tends to carry both jobs, a new logo can slow the anchor when it is paying the bills. As an operator, I would track field hours and unplanned engineering time across comparable deployments, the measure Symbotic’s filings can’t give outsiders. When design engineers keep getting pulled in to solve problems already solved at earlier sites, the product is still in development. It’s ready to scale once the team can predict and price the engineering and field work each new site requires.

Symbotic’s timeline is a reason to start testing with a second customer well before the anchor’s rollout slows. An early project with a defined scope and budget can show how much effort another account really takes. Rajat Bhageria of Chef Robotics has described combining multiple customers’ requirements into one product specification and charging modest non-recurring engineering fees before building. That way, several buyers shape one product without a one-off project for each. Adding accounts for revenue is a different decision, because it commits people. It belongs after the team can estimate what a new site takes and deliver it alongside existing projects.

Exol and Walmex also change how I would size a customer base. A buyer owned or funded by an existing partner tends to move with that partner, so independent budgets tell me more than the number of logos. AutoStore reached about 1,300 end customers through 23 distribution partners in fiscal 2025, yet four partners supplied 74% of its revenue. Concentration tends to move more easily than it disappears, so the real choice is which kind the company can survive.

Before hiring ahead of anchor demand, it pays to model two scenarios. One is a six-month pause in the rollout. The other is the rollout finishing on schedule, the no-villain case above, which tends to get left out of plans because it looks like success.

A Bossa Nova mobile shelf-scanning robot at work in a Walmart store. Source: Bossa Nova Robotics

What not to copy

The lesson I would leave behind is the concentration itself. Symbotic’s founder, Rick Cohen, also chairs C&S Wholesale Grocers, which gave Symbotic access to production environments during development, and Walmart later funded development directly. A startup whose anchor offers neither kind of support is making a different bet with the same percentage.

I’d also look at the financial strength of both the robotics company and the business supporting it. In agricultural robotics, Root AI became part of a grower when AppHarvest bought it in 2021. AppHarvest and its robotics subsidiary entered Chapter 11 in 2023, and the group’s court declaration pointed to farming losses and financing pressure. Zordi’s chief executive later announced that the company had bought AppHarvest’s robotics IP and assets, but the record doesn’t show whether Root AI could have stood on its own. Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021, a year in which its apple-growing partner, T&G Global, stayed profitable, and its chief executive said the company couldn’t raise enough investment to finish development. Root AI went down with its parent company, and Abundant ran out of investors before it could finish its harvester.

Walmart was also the main customer for Bossa Nova Robotics, a Carnegie Mellon spinout. By November 2020, Walmart had ended its relationship with the company, whose shelf-scanning robots had reached about 500 stores. Earlier that year, the companies had announced plans to reach 1,000 stores. The Wall Street Journal reported that employees picking online orders were giving Walmart another way to monitor inventory.

The Journal’s sources added that Walmart U.S. CEO John Furner had concerns about how shoppers reacted to robots in stores. One of them said Walmart told Bossa Nova it saw an improvement in stores with the robots, “but we don’t see enough of an improvement” in revenue and other metrics. Bossa Nova laid off about half its staff after the contract ended. It later shifted toward retail AI that could use images captured on phones, and the company eventually closed. I read Walmart’s decision as a reason to keep testing the customer’s alternatives as its operations change. A robot can keep doing its assigned job even as the customer finds less reason to pay for it.

Symbotic’s fiscal 2025 annual report says the contracts behind its backlog lack termination-for-convenience clauses. Most of that backlog can be terminated only for missed performance standards, insolvency, or specified changes in control. A founder can sort an anchor’s demand into orders the contract commits it to and expansion it can still walk away from. Hiring against that expansion means carrying those salaries if the orders don’t come, possibly for as long as it takes a new customer to go live.

About the author

Deepak Jayaraj is the vice president of hardware engineering and manufacturing at Four Growers, an agricultural robotics company based in Pittsburgh. With over 15 years of experience spanning space robotics, medical devices, and AgTech, he specializes in guiding robotics companies through the critical transition from prototype to scaled deployment and the economics of hardware business models.

]]> Key Takeaways
  • WorldOracle is a benchmark for action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) that scores each model’s predicted rollout against the paired real-world execution, with both starting from the same initial observations and following the same action sequence.
  • Seven representative models were evaluated; arm motion was predicted relatively well, but object positions and movements often deviated from reality, and performance dropped over complete operation sequences.
  • The platform opened to developers on October 16 and accepts both open-weight and closed-source models.

In one WorldOracle case, the robot’s grasp missed, yet the world model predicted a successful pick. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

In one case showcased by WorldOracle, a robot’s grasp missed, yet the world model predicted that the robot had successfully picked up the fruit.

Given the initial frame and action sequence of a real manipulation episode, the model generated a rollout that looked plausible on screen but differed from the actual execution. The success it depicted never happened in reality.

Researchers from Princeton University, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Toronto, NVIDIA and AgiBot have jointly introduced WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) by comparing their predictions with real-world executions that start from the same initial observations and follow the same action sequences.

The team evaluated seven representative models — among them DreamDojo, Cosmos 3, IRASim and GE-Sim 2.0 — and identified two prominent problems. First, while the motion paths of robot arms are predicted relatively well, the positions and movements of manipulated objects can still deviate from reality. Second, models that perform well over short horizons can degrade significantly over complete operation sequences.

On October 16, WorldOracle, an evaluation platform for action-conditioned world models, officially opened to developers. The research team has collected real manipulation episodes in advance, recording both video and actions. Developers use the initial frames and action sequences provided in the evaluation set to generate predicted videos and submit them to the platform, which scores each submission against the corresponding real execution record. The results show whether a model has accurately predicted the consequences of the actions, helping developers pinpoint weaknesses and verify improvements.

Project page: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18826

How Do Seven World Models Perform?
Arm motion is right, but objects don’t always follow

The predicted motion of a robot arm reaching toward a piece of fruit and closing its gripper may closely match its actual motion, yet the model can still incorrectly predict whether the fruit is lifted and where it moves next. To assess the two separately, the research team compared the position and motion of the robot arm and of the manipulated object in each predicted video against the real-world recording, and scored them individually.

Spatial alignment scores for the robot arm and the manipulated object. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

The results show that all five models evaluated on the human-operated AgiBot G2 data scored higher on the arm than on the object. In other words, even when the arm in the generated video follows the given actions well, the position and movement of the object may still depart from reality. IRASim scored 78.8 on the robot arm but only 29.1 on the manipulated object, while Cosmos 3 scored 89.4 and 45.4, respectively. The remaining models showed gaps of varying size.

Accuracy declines as the rollout horizon grows

Time presents a second challenge. Completing a continuous task often requires multiple grasps, placements and adjustments, and the object state left by one interaction becomes the starting point for the next. Whether a model stays close to reality must therefore be tested over the full process.

WorldOracle evaluates both the first 30 seconds of each trajectory and the complete long sequence.

WorldOracle-SV scores of the same models under the two evaluation horizons. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

On the same set of AgiBot G2 teleoperation data, the WorldOracle-SV scores of all five models fell. DreamDojo dropped from 50.56 to 27.08, and Cosmos 3 from 53.99 to 26.60, nearly halving in both cases. GE-Sim 2.0 fell from 73.86 to 63.33; it posted the highest score of the five models at both horizons and the smallest decline over the full sequence.

The relative ranking also shifted. IRASim scored below Ctrl-World, DreamDojo and Cosmos 3 over the first 30 seconds, but above all three over the full sequence.

What Can WorldOracle Measure?

WorldOracle evaluation framework: real actions are recorded, the model predicts what follows, and the result is scored against the real execution. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

Accurately predicting a failure earns a high score

WorldOracle starts from pre-collected records of real manipulation. A model is given the initial frame and the action sequence and generates a predicted video, which is compared with the real execution of the same actions.

What models must predict includes missed grasps, drops and spills. If an operation fails in reality, accurately predicting that failure counts as a correct prediction.

Failed executions therefore serve as an important class of test samples: they reveal whether a model follows the given actions and their consequences, or defaults to a successful version of the task.

The benchmark covers two robot embodiments, AgiBot G2 and YAM, as well as first-person human-hand manipulation. Four tasks (fruit picking, towel hanging, water pouring and drawer pulling) involve interaction with rigid, deformable, fluid and articulated objects, respectively. Task coverage varies by embodiment, as defined in the evaluation set.

The human-hand setting is intended for world models that can accept hand-motion input, testing whether a model can predict subsequent object changes and interaction outcomes from a recorded sequence of hand poses. Models with egocentric world-modeling capabilities are evaluated zero-shot in this setting, without any additional hand-adaptation data provided by the platform.

Real execution footage for the four task types. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

The data come from two sources. The first is human-operated data collection, including robot teleoperation trajectories and human hand-manipulation trajectories. The second is policy rollouts, in which an autonomous policy controls a real robot.

When a robot executes autonomously, it can produce pauses, jitter and motion corrections that differ from human operation. Including such data helps test whether a world model remains accurate when faced with actions from different sources.

The platform offers three tracks:

  • WorldOracle-Core: evaluates predictions over the first 30 seconds of human-operated trajectories.
  • WorldOracle-Policy: evaluates predictions over complete episodes of autonomous policy rollouts on AgiBot G2.
  • WorldOracle-Long: evaluates sustained prediction over complete, human-operated long sequences.

The WorldOracle study compares several embodied world-model benchmarks. Of these, WorldOracle is the only one that simultaneously covers action-sequence input, real-world execution data, failure cases, long-horizon interaction, multiple embodiments, multi-view evaluation and autonomous policy rollouts.

Breaking down prediction error: outcomes and process

The predicted and real robot arm positions may closely match even when the model gets the fruit’s grasp state wrong; two final states may look alike while the paths that led to them differ. A single score can hardly capture such differences.

WorldOracle checks predictions with four complementary metrics:

  • Physical State Correctness: checks whether object positions, grasp states and liquid transfer at the end of each interaction match the real outcome.
  • Interaction Spatial Alignment: checks whether the positions and movement paths of objects, robot arms or human hands are consistent with the real process.
  • Key Interaction Area Fidelity: focuses on regions such as the object, gripper and hand, combining pixel-level, perceptual and semantic similarity to reduce the influence of large background areas on the score.
  • Multi-View Action Coherence: for models that support multi-view output, checks whether robot motion across synchronized camera views is aligned with the real execution.

The first three metrics are averaged with equal weights to form the WorldOracle-SV (single-view) score; for multi-view evaluation, the fourth metric is added and the four are again equally weighted. Sub-scores are also retained, allowing developers to distinguish problems in state prediction, motion trajectories and local detail.

To validate the metrics, the researchers asked 119 participants to compare 128 pairs of predicted videos. The four metrics agreed with human choices on which prediction was better 88.1% to 93.2% of the time.

The researchers also note the benchmark’s limits. It measures how closely a prediction matches a single recorded real execution. For fluids, deformable objects and stochastic contact, the same action can lead to several plausible outcomes, and a single reference cannot fully describe that range.

Training support also differs across embodiments: AgiBot G2 models use a benchmark-specific training set, YAM models use public data, and the human-hand setting is evaluated zero-shot. Scores across the three settings should therefore not be used directly to judge embodiment difficulty or cross-embodiment generalization.

How Can Developers Participate?
Open submissions give model iteration concrete feedback

WorldOracle supports both open-weight and closed-source models. After registration and approval, developers choose a track according to the embodiment or manipulation setting their model supports, generate and upload predicted videos following the submission guide, and view composite scores, sub-scores and comparisons.

For model iteration, this feedback can be tied to specific questions: Did a change make object motion more accurate? Did it reduce incorrect predictions of failed operations? Does the improvement still hold as the prediction horizon grows?

Whether the futures generated by a world model can be relied upon must be tested against real execution. WorldOracle turns that test into a unified set of tasks, data and scoring methods, giving developers a basis for comparing models, identifying errors and verifying improvements.

]]>

The first Data Factory hub is set to become one of Europe’s largest physical AI training facilities for humanoid robots. | Source: Generative Bionics

Generative Bionics this week announced plans to build a proprietary, multi-site “Physical AI Data Factory” in Italy. The company said the new 5,000-sq.-m (53,819.5-sq.-ft.) hub will help move humanoid robotics from laboratory demonstrations to reliable industrial deployment.

In addition, Generative Bionics said it hopes to advance European humanoid sovereignty, ensuring that the data, models, and know-how behind Europe’s industrial humanoids are generated, trained and validated on the continent.

“The value that Europe has right now is within its industry, and we have to extract physical AI data in order to train our own models,” Daniele Pucci, the CEO of Generative Bionics, told The Robot Report. “This is a competitive advantage that Europe right now has, because of the automation that we have been putting in place over the last 40 years.”

Generative Bionics said the new facility will be operational by the fourth quarter of 2027. The Genoa, Italy-based company plans to eventually open a second facility elsewhere in Europe and a third serving global markets. Together, the three facilities will reproduce real industrial environments, generate high-fidelity physical data, and connect that data with large-scale simulation.

Building on their strategic technology collaboration, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. will be Generative Bionics’ AI infrastructure partner, and the Physical AI Data Factory network will be powered by AMD Helios. Its rack-scale architecture will provide the compute foundation to process physical and synthetic data, train physical AI models, and run thousands of digital-twin scenario variations in parallel.

Data Factory to test GENE.01 in a range of industries

The Physical AI Data Factory will connect real-world robot operations, simulation and AI development in a continuous real-to-sim-to-real cycle, said Generative Bionics. The company said this will allow it to configure and validate its GENE.01 humanoid robot for specific industrial environments before customer deployment, then feed data from deployed fleets into future training cycles.

Industrial humanoids must learn from the conditions they will encounter at work, noted the Generative Bionics. This requires data that captures contact, force, motion, proximity, temperature, task constraints, and human interaction in realistic operating settings. For GENE.01, the dataset will include vision and motion data as well as signals captured through its full-body multimodal skin.

“A robot is not only vision and is not only language,” said Pucci. “It is position, velocity, acceleration, temperature, and contact forces, so there is a large variety of data that you have to take into account.”

The Data Factory will reproduce environments selected with industrial partners and allow fleets of GENE.01 robots to perform tasks continuously in real-world conditions. These operations will generate high-fidelity physical data for training world action models (WAM) and validating the complete robot system, including perception, control, safety behavior, and task execution, before deployment at customer sites.

Each physical environment and robot configuration will also be recreated as a digital twin. The same tasks can then be repeated across thousands of variations in layout, objects, materials, operating conditions, and failure modes that would be impractical to reproduce physically. Models trained and tested in simulation will be deployed back to the robots for validation, while data from physical operations will feed the next training cycle.

Generative Bionics wants to help find robot ‘ChatGPT moment’

Large language models (LLMs) learn from vast amounts of information available online, noted Generative Bionics. Humanoid robots have no comparable source of data on how to act in the physical world.

The Physical AI Data Factory will create such a source by collecting data as GENE.01 performs industrial tasks and expanding those experiences through digital-twins running on AMD compute.

“We have the ambition of being the European champion in physical AI, and even robotics, designed to scale globally,” said Pucci. “That’s our clear positioning, and for this, we are taking a close look at the supply chain that can supply our future manufacturing.”

“Manufacturing here is divided into three levels: the manufacturing of data, the manufacturing of robots, and the manufacturing of models,” she continued. Pucci said if Europe wants to achieve sovereignty in this area, it needs to invest in all three.

Right now, humanoid robots from China have been garnering a lot of attention with flashy demos and large funding rounds. But, Pucci, notes that this doesn’t mean the country is necessarily ahead of Europe.

“I want to be crystal clear about this. Many of the Chinese robots that are out there are simply not certified to enter industrial settings,” Pucci said. “The narrative that the Chinese solved as the issues is very far from reality.”

“Right now, we believe that many of the existing solutions are basically for entertainment, and this is a market segment that we respect,” she added. “But, Generative Bionics is taking the issue of safety and certification very seriously because we want to go B2B first.”

GENE.01 can be customized for specific applications

Generative Bionics claimed that a few things separate its platform from the average humanoid robot. To start, GENE.01 features full-body tactile sensing.

“It comes naturally to give the humanoid robots the sense of touch, because humanoid robots have to perceive people not only while talking, but also while interacting with them physically,” Pucci said. “That’s why GENE was given this unique multimodal scheme, which can perceive not only the sense of touch but also the sense of proximity.”

Generative Bionics also plans to offer GENE.01 as a base platform that can be customized for different industries.

“We have a clear view that humanoid robots cannot be used for anything that comes to your mind, because a humanoid robot welding in a shipyard cannot be the same as a humanoid robot in healthcare,” noted Pucci. “There is a fundamental difference in the development cycle.”

The company has three levels of customization. “The first one is the AI, because a robot moving boxes does not need the same AI of a robot in healthcare,” said Pucci. “The second is the exterior design. In the shipyard, you have to be resistant against high temperatures, sparks, and powders. The third is the hands and the feet.”

“This is really scalable at the manufacturing level, because you have a common platform, and then you can customize at the end the so-called end of lines at these three levels,” she continued. “This is basically the same approach that you have in automotive.”

Generative Bionics is building on more than 20 years of research, development, and prototyping of humanoids at the Italian Institute of Technology (IIT). The company spun out of IIT in 2024, and IIT has granted it exclusive licenses to key technologies.

Dream Labs said its models learn how the physical world works from video and can control new robots without any data. | Source: Dream Labs

More brains are coming for robots. Dream Labs this week said it has raised $90 million in seed funding. The company also launched Dream API, a publicly available application programming interface to turn a robot’s camera feed and a plain-English instructions into motor commands, even for robots it has never seen before.

Factories worldwide run a record 5 million industrial robots, yet nearly every one is programmed for a single task, and most cannot transfer what they have learned to other machines, noted Dream Labs. Low-cost robots now sell for a few thousand dollars but ship with no built-in intelligence. Teaching one robot one task can take specialists months, and a new task or new hardware often means starting from zero, according to the San Francisco startup.

Dream Labs said its Dream-1 flagship model works across robots from different manufacturers. Trained on video of people performing everyday tasks, it can predict what will happen next and determine the robot’s resulting action. Because it learns from video rather than from a single machine, its capabilities transfer across hardware, Dream Labs claimed.

The company said Dream-1 can control any robot “out of the box” with grippers and zero-shot learning.

“The hardware is ready. What’s been missing is a brain any robot can use,” stated Joel Jang, co-founder and CEO of Dream Labs. “When you get into a rental car, you don’t relearn how to drive. You find the controls, and your past driving experience does the rest.”

“Dream-1 approaches a new robot the same way, so a new robot can do useful work in minutes, not months,” he added. “And instead of edited demos, we’re giving people a working model they can test themselves, mistakes included.”

B Capital and Kindred Ventures led the round. It also included participation from A.Capital, Unusual Ventures, SV Angel, Wing VC, Scribble VC, and Adrian Aoun, among others.

Inside Dream Labs’ product portfolio

Developers and robot enthusiasts can start using Dream Labs’ AI products today. The company said Dream API translates visual inputs and natural language prompts directly into robot actions.

Developers can sign up, connect any robots with grippers, and the robot will carry out the task. Dream Labs runs its models in data centers around the world, so robots respond quickly wherever they are.

The company also offers fine-tuning as a service. For unsupported hardware or new capabilities, developers and robot makers can submit a small batch of demonstration data to receive a tailored model within hours.

Developers also have access to Dream Labs’ robot playground. Anyone with a browser can type commands to a robot in Dream Labs’ San Francisco office and watch it respond live and unedited, no robot purchase required.

“A capable robot arm has gone from the price of a luxury car to the price of a high-end laptop. What it needs now is intelligence,” said Daisy Cai, general partner at B Capital. “This team did some of the defining work in robot learning at NVIDIA. Now anyone with an API key can build on it.”

Startup works with more than 20 hardware partners

Dream Labs supports robots today that cost between about $2,000 and $10,000. Dream-1 needs no extra data to control a two-armed robot with parallel grippers.

For its over 20 hardware partners, Dream Labs said it goes beyond that baseline, refining the model for each robot so it performs at its best. Dream-1 currently handles tabletop tasks such as picking and placing objects and folding laundry, with support for wheeled mobile robots and dexterous hands to follow.

The company said it plans use the new funding primarily for compute as it expands the tasks and robots Dream-1 can handle, and scales to support more users.

“Our customers buy our robots to build things, and the hardest part has always been getting them to do actual work,” said Ryan Chan, co-founder and CEO of MakerMods, which sells $2,000 bimanual robot arms. “With Dream-1, our robot was up and running in a few minutes and attempting tasks we never programmed. We can focus on building better hardware, and our customers get intelligence that keeps improving.”

]]> German startups are increasingly looking towards Japan as a destination for international expansion, industrial partnerships and technological cooperation.

From DefenceTech and nuclear fusion to quantum computing and space infrastructure, recent developments suggest that Tokyo is becoming an important partner for some of Europe’s most ambitious technology companies.

This momentum became particularly visible today, during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Japan. Munich-based Proxima Fusion announced two Japanese partnerships, while drone manufacturer Quantum Systems unveiled agreements with Mitsubishi Chemical and Panasonic, alongside plans to establish a permanent presence in Tokyo.

The announcements form part of a wider diplomatic push. According to Japanese news agency Jiji Press, Germany and Japan were expected to sign 33 memoranda of understanding (MoUs) spanning AI, nuclear fusion and other advanced technologies.

However, the more interesting story for Europe’s startup ecosystem extends beyond a single diplomatic visit.

More than handshakes

For Quantum Systems, the visit marks a step towards becoming an established player in Japan’s DefenceTech market.

Founded in 2015 in Gilching by Florian Seibel, Michael Kriegel, Tobias Kloss and Armin Busse, Quantum Systems develops unmanned aerial systems and software for defence, security and civilian applications.

The company announced the establishment of Quantum Systems Japan K.K., including a Tokyo office, alongside MoUs with Mitsubishi Chemical and Panasonic. The agreements aim to combine Japanese manufacturing capabilities with German drone technology, strengthening local supply chains and bringing Quantum Systems closer to Japanese customers.

Sven Kruck, co-CEO of Quantum Systems, said: “Japan has understood where defence is heading: unmanned systems, rapid innovation and the industrial capacity to deliver at scale. Ukraine has shown why this matters. When personnel are scarce and threats evolve fast, technological advantage is decisive. Japan’s manufacturing strength and our operational experience are a powerful combination. We are proud to put down roots in Japan and honoured to help strengthen its defence industrial base.”

Meanwhile, Munich-based Proxima Fusion, founded in 2023 as a spin-out from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, announced two separate agreements involving fusion energy.

As EU-Startups reported earlier today, its agreement with Kyoto Fusioneering focuses on plasma-heating systems and fuel-cycle technologies. A separate agreement with Fujikura explores industrial-scale manufacturing of superconducting tape in Lower Saxony, building on a previously announced €140 million manufacturing initiative.

The cooperation also extends into space. Established German aerospace group OHB signed an MoU with Japanese space-tech company Astroscale, founded in 2013, to explore opportunities in orbital servicing, surveillance and space security. Astroscale, on the same day, also announced a €17 million (£15 million) MOD Contract from the UK Government.

Tokyo was already calling

The latest announcements are part of a broader trend we’v seen here at EU-Startups.

Munich-based defence AI startup Helsing, founded in 2021, has already been pursuing opportunities in Japan. In August 2026, Reuters reported that Japanese conglomerate Rakuten was helping Helsing pursue a potential contract to supply unmanned systems to Japan’s military. Its HX-2 strike drone was undergoing testing by Japan’s Ground Self-Defence Forces.

Industrial cooperation has also attracted Japanese capital into Germany. In March 2025, Panasonic announced a €30 million equity investment in Munich-based tado°, founded in 2011, expanding an existing partnership combining Panasonic’s heat pumps with tado°’s smart heating controls and energy management software.

Quantum computing provides another example. Braunschweig-based QUDORA Technologies, founded in 2021, established a Japanese subsidiary and partnered with Fixstars in May 2026 to make its quantum computing tools accessible through a cloud platform.

By October, QUDORA Japan had been selected for a government-backed research project alongside Kyocera and Japan’s National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology.

Even outside DeepTech, German companies have recognised the opportunity. Cologne-based translation technology company DeepL, founded in 2017, established a Japanese subsidiary in 2023 to strengthen its local commercial operations.

These developments suggest that Japanese partnerships are becoming an increasingly deliberate part of German startups’ international strategies.

Why Japan, why now?

Japan’s strengths in electronics, robotics, precision engineering, advanced materials and industrial manufacturing offer European startups capabilities that can be difficult and expensive to develop independently.

For companies building fusion reactors, quantum computers or advanced robotics, access to established manufacturers and specialised suppliers may be just as valuable as attracting new customers.

Japan has also been working to strengthen its startup ecosystem. Its five-year startup development plan, introduced in 2022, set an ambitious objective of increasing annual startup investment to approximately €56 billion (¥10 trillion) by the 2027 financial year.

Meanwhile, cooperation between Brussels and Tokyo is expanding. In May 2026, the EU and Japan agreed to deepen collaboration in AI, quantum technology, semiconductors, digital infrastructure and cross-border data flows.

The Tokyo test

Despite the momentum, Japan is not necessarily an easy market to enter.

Language barriers, different business practices, complex procurement processes and the importance of long-term corporate relationships can make expansion challenging, particularly for startups with limited resources.

The experiences of Quantum Systems, Helsing and QUDORA highlight one possible solution: finding established Japanese partners rather than attempting to navigate the market independently.

German startups appear to have recognised the opportunity Japan offers foreign tech and talent. The question now is whether the rest of Europe will follow.

The post German startups are betting big on Japan. Should the rest of Europe follow? appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Magic Vision, an Italian DeepTech startup developing AI and computer vision technologies to monitor and support older people and vulnerable individuals, has closed a €600k funding round.

Investors include SixS, the Italian company behind Gecos, a management software platform for the nonprofit sector, alongside a group of Italian business angels with expertise in law, compliance and business development.

“Population ageing is putting pressure on care systems, which must meet growing needs with increasingly limited resources and staff. Technology can make a practical contribution by enabling continuous monitoring and timely intervention when needed,” says Lorenzo Mauri, co-founder and CEO of Magic Vision.

Magic Vision’s funding comes alongside several European investments in technology-enabled care during 2026.

Germany’s Patronus raised €11 million for its elderly emergency-response technology, while Spain’s Tucuvi secured €17 million for AI-powered nursing follow-up and Portugal’s Hope Care closed a €6 million round for remote patient monitoring.

Together with Magic Vision, these account for approximately €34.6 million in funding. In Italy, Rome-based VoiceMed reported reaching €1 million in cumulative funding for its device-free respiratory monitoring technology.

“Wearable devices, emergency buttons and other available systems had significant limitations. We therefore decided to use our expertise in artificial intelligence to develop technology capable of recognising risks without requiring a person to wear a device or call for help,” adds Federico Lanzani, co-founder and CTO of Magic Vision.

Magic Vision is an Italian startup founded in 2023 by six co-founders with expertise in AI and computer vision. Based in Meda, in the province of Monza and Brianza, it develops Silver Eye, an environmental monitoring system for older people and vulnerable individuals, designed to support their independence and assist families and care professionals.

Silver Eye uses proprietary AI and computer vision algorithms to analyse people’s activity and rest patterns , identify behavioural anomalies and detect critical events such as falls. Operating through environmental sensors without wearable devices, the system enable individual behavioural monitoring even in dynamic, shared settings, including senior living facilities, cohousing and private homes.

The technology is designed to protect privacy: data is processed locally using edge AI, without storing or transmitting images. Rather than functioning as a video surveillance system, it​ analyses the information needed to identify potential risks, alerting caregivers only when necessary.

The aim is to support prevention and help older people maintain their independence, providing technology for care models ranging from shared housing and home care to traditional residential and nursing care facilities.

During its growth journey, the startup has benefited from incubation at PoliHub and support from ComoNExT’s NExT Accelerator and Paradigma Exponential Hub , which helped connect the founders with investors. It has also received a €30k award from the Milan Monza Brianza Lodi Chamber of Commerce through the Switch2Product programme.

The funding has enabled Magic Vision to complete development and bring Silver Eye to market.

Already deployed in pilot and commercial projects with Italian care providers, Silver Eye has more than 200 sensors installed, with a target of monitoring over 100 people by the end of 2026.

“The idea for Silver Eye came from a personal experience: when my grandfather fell and remained on the floor for an entire day, I started looking for a solution that could prevent something similar from happening again,” says Federico.

The company is also preparing a €1.5 million funding round to accelerate commercial growth, build a network of partners and distributors across Italy, and begin its European expansion, with the aim of securing its first international customer within 24 months.
