Recorded Series A–C investment rose by approximately 66% in the first nine months of 2026, yet funding in rounds worth €22.2 million to less than €88.9 million declined by around 8%. This middle segment is particularly important for AI startups moving beyond […]

The post OPINION: Scaling is the real test of Europe’s AI boom appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Europe’s AI funding boom is not benefiting every part of the market equally. Recorded Series A–C investment rose by approximately 66% in the first nine months of 2026, yet funding in rounds worth €22.2 million to less than €88.9 million declined by around 8%.

This middle segment is particularly important for AI startups moving beyond their first customers. Expanding internationally, hiring teams and securing larger enterprise contracts can require substantial capital, even for companies operating on a much smaller scale than Europe’s leading AI developers.

The contrasting funding trends raise questions about how Europe’s next generation of AI companies will finance their expansion. While overall investment continues to grow, the more important test may be whether startups can progress from early funding rounds to sustainable businesses without becoming overly dependent on their next investment.

The findings are based on an analysis of Crunchbase funding-round data for the first nine months of 2025 and 2026, using consistent dates and funding stages and correcting identified data issues. The original dollar-based categories were retained, with euro thresholds rounded for readability. Figures follow Crunchbase’s classifications and currency conversions and may differ from public announcements.

How Europe’s AI funding splits across the market

The adjusted Crunchbase sample recorded approximately €15.04 billion in announced Series A–C funding in the first nine months of 2026, up from €9.06 billion a year earlier. The number of recorded funding events increased from 203 to 232. Of these, 196 events in 2025 and 218 in 2026 were included in the round-size breakdown. These figures cover companies tagged as Artificial Intelligence by Crunchbase and do not represent all European AI funding stages.

The growth was concentrated in larger transactions. Rounds worth €88.9 million or more increased from 18 to 33, accounting for approximately 74% of disclosed funding in 2026, up from 59% the previous year. Although the ten biggest investments represented about half of the total, funding outside these transactions also grew.

Smaller rounds became more frequent, increasing from 108 to 124 for investments below €22.2 million. The middle of the market, however, moved in the opposite direction. The €22.2–88.9 million segment saw its share of disclosed funding fall from approximately 29% to 16%. Across all rounds below €88.9 million, recorded funding barely increased, growing by just 2.7% to €3.86 billion.

This uneven growth suggests that Europe’s AI investment boom has not been felt equally across different funding sizes. While more smaller rounds were recorded and large investments attracted substantial capital, the segment between them contracted.

Some of the largest announcements also require caution. NEURA Robotics announced a Series C of up to €1.24 billion, while Multiverse Computing described a round targeting up to €500 million. Excluding both amounts reduced the sample’s overall funding growth from approximately 66% to 47%.

The increase therefore remained substantial even without these transactions, but the headline amounts should not be interpreted as confirmation that all the funding had already been received.

From €98 million to €3 billion: The different costs of scaling AI

Taktile, a Berlin-founded company developing decision technology for financial institutions, raised approximately €51 million in a Series B in February 2025. By June 2026, it had secured another approximately €98 million in Series C funding. The company operates in enterprise software, where expansion means winning more customers and making its technology work inside complex banking systems. 

Mistral raised €3 billion in a Series D in September 2026. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous computing resources and research investment. The financing needs of these two companies differ considerably, yet their announcements contribute to the broader picture of an AI funding boom. These examples provide context separately from the statistical sample: Taktile is absent from the European-headquartered export, and Mistral’s Series D falls outside the stages analysed. 

Funding activity also increased across all three stages. Series A events rose from 133 to 148, Series B from 51 to 58, and Series C from 19 to 26. Median round sizes grew at every stage, with the most pronounced increase at Series C, where the median rose from €49.3 million to €93.3 million.

These figures do not indicate a broad decline in Series B or C activity. However, they cannot show how easily individual companies secured funding or what conditions investors attached to their investments.

Taktile shows that companies can successfully move through successive funding stages. For other founders, planning that transition means making expensive decisions before they know when the next round will arrive or what terms investors will offer.

The cost of depending on your next funding round

A company may raise capital to enter new markets, hire sales teams and expand its customer base. These plans often assume that another funding round will follow once the business reaches its next growth targets. But expansion can become expensive long before the company reaches those targets.

For an enterprise AI business, new contracts may require extensive customisation and ongoing engineering support. Revenue grows, yet the company spends more than expected to deliver it. Hiring commitments and operating costs continue even when progress falls behind the original plan.

This leaves founders in a difficult position. If they need fresh capital to maintain operations, they have less control over the timing of fundraising and the terms investors offer. A more measured expansion strategy may look less impressive in the short term, but it gives management greater freedom to choose when and how to raise its next round.

The next test for Europe’s AI boom

The next test for Europe’s AI funding market will come in 2027 and 2028, when some of the startups raising smaller amounts today will need substantially more capital to expand. Whether they can secure investments of €27 million, €44 million or more on favourable terms will help determine their ability to grow.

The current data does not show how many companies sought funding unsuccessfully, how long fundraising took or how much capital they needed. It therefore cannot establish a shortage of growth capital across Europe.

The next stage will also put more pressure on business fundamentals. Enterprise AI companies that can retain customers and expand without a corresponding rise in operating costs should have an advantage when seeking further investment. Others may face difficult choices about how quickly they can grow and how much capital they can afford to raise.

It will be worth following the companies that secured smaller rounds in 2025 and 2026. Their progression to larger investments, the time between funding rounds and the terms they receive will help establish whether Europe has a genuine growth-capital constraint.

Europe may continue setting AI investment records. The more consequential development over the next few years will be how many of today’s funded startups manage to reach the next stage and build sustainable businesses. That is where the depth of Europe’s AI funding market will become much clearer.

The post OPINION: Scaling is the real test of Europe’s AI boom appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> AP Ventures, a London-based independent VC firm investing in early-stage industrial and energy technologies, today announced the final close of AP Ventures Fund III LP (Fund III). 

The VC firm has raised €269.62 million ($300 million) in commitments for Fund III from a “diverse group” of existing and new institutional investors, including sovereign wealth funds, corporates, pension funds, and family offices. Since its initial close in 2024, Fund III has backed 13 portfolio companies developing technologies focused on industrial and energy systems.

“This final close reflects the confidence our existing and new investors place in AP Ventures’ ability to identify and support exceptional technology companies. Strong support from returning investors, alongside new institutional partners, allows us to keep backing the technologies industry needs to operate more productively and securely, from the materials it depends on to the processes and data that run it,” said Andrew Hinkly, Founder and Managing Partner at AP Ventures.

AP Ventures began as part of Anglo American Platinum’s PGM (Platinum Group Metal) Investment Programme, and in 2018 it launched as an independent venture capital fund to invest in PGM applications. As cornerstone investors, Anglo American Platinum and South Africa’s Public Investment Corporation (PIC) each committed $100 million to AP Ventures.

Anglo American Platinum Limited is a member of the Anglo American plc Group and is the world’s leading primary producer of platinum group metals, whereas the Public Investment Corporation (PIC) is a public asset management firm wholly owned by the South African government, with the Minister of Finance as the sole shareholder representative of the government.  

Led by Hinkly and Kevin Eggers, AP Ventures invests globally in early-stage technologies reshaping the industrial economy, including advanced materials, industrial processes, and energy systems.

According to the firm, this fundraise comes as demand accelerates for high-performing infrastructure across energy and industry. It notes that development and operations of industrial and energy systems are being reshaped by rising power demand, tightening supply chains for critical minerals and materials, and the growing role of AI, data and automation in industrial operations. This creates a growing opportunity for technologies that boost productivity and strengthen supply security, AP Ventures says.

Fund III invests in early-stage technology companies and works alongside founders through commercialisation, industrial deployment and scale-up.  Its strategic focus spans low-carbon molecules, including hydrogen, across production, storage, transport and end use; carbon capture and utilisation; and circularity and advanced recycling, with applications in energy-intensive, hard-to-abate sectors such as chemicals, steel, aviation and heavy mobility.

Its present portfolio of 13 companies includes: 

Teragen Energy: a Southborough-based startup that develops metal-supported solid oxide fuel cells that can provide clean, on-site power for data centres and other critical infrastructure.

]]> Proxima Fusion, a German stellarator fusion company, has today signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in Japan to strengthen the industrial supply chain behind Germany’s ambition to become a global leader in fusion energy. 

The MoU was signed during Chancellor Merz’s visit to Japan with Kyoto Fusioneering, a Japanese fusion technology provider, and marks the cooperation of critical technologies needed to build and operate commercial fusion power plants.

Dr. Francesco Sciortino, co-founder and CEO of Proxima Fusion, said: “The global race to fusion will be won in factories and supply chains. Japan has spent decades building world-class fusion engineering capabilities; Germany has the leading stellarator engineering in the world and knows how to industrialise. In working closely with Kyoto Fusioneering and Fujikura, we are building a new industry together, one that makes both our countries more secure.

“Japanese partners choosing to work with Germany is a direct result of the strong backing fusion enjoys from the German government and the European Union, as well as our determination to apply world-leading technology to the world’s increasing energy demands and climate challenge.”

Today’s news comes off the tail-end of a spectacular couple of years for the Munich-based startup.

EU-Startups has followed Proxima Fusion’s development since its €7 million pre-Seed round in 2023, followed by a €20 million Seed round in 2024 and a €130 million Series A in June 2025, extended by a further €15 million that September. In July 2026, the company secured another €411 million, bringing its reported funding and public grants to more than €650 million and supporting the development of its Alpha demonstration stellarator.

This progression comes amid investment in other European fusion technologies, including fellow Munich-based Marvel Fusion’s €50 million Series B extension in 2025 and Bristol-based Astral Systems’ €26 million Series A in 2026, the latter focused on medical-isotope applications.

Together with Proxima’s latest round, they represent €487 million in investment across 2025–2026, reflecting the varied European approach to fusion power.

Kiyoshi Seko, Representative Director, President and COO, Kyoto Fusioneering, said: “Germany is approaching fusion not only as a future source of energy, but as a pillar of its High-Tech Agenda to build national prosperity through advanced technology. Manufacturing and engineering are at the heart of that vision, and they are also at the heart of what Kyoto Fusioneering does. Through our cooperation with Proxima Fusion, we will bring our state of the art plasma heating.. technologies to one of the most ambitious stellarator programmes in the world, and help turn fusion into a real industry in Germany.“

Founded in 2023, Proxima Fusion is a spin-out from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics. The company is developing commercial fusion power plants based on the QI-HTS stellarator concept. With Alpha, Proxima is developing a net-energy fusion demonstrator targeted for the early 2030s, paving the way for Stellaris, the world’s first commercial stellarator fusion power plant later that decade.

On the other side of the MoU sits Kyoto Fusioneering, a premier fusion technology and integrated systems developer. It delivers technologies and engineering services for plasma heating, tritium fuel cycle, and tritium breeding blanket and thermal cycle systems that are essential to advanced fusion programmes worldwide, regardless of confinement approach.

Under the MoU, the two companies will continue and expand joint work on next-generation gyrotrons for plasma heating and on fuel cycle technologies. Kyoto Fusioneering will also contribute its technologies and engineering expertise to the commercialisation and industrial deployment of fusion energy in Germany, including within the national Fusion Hubs initiative of the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space’s (BMFTR). 

The German federal government has set the goal of building the world’s first fusion power plant in Germany. Turning that ambition into reality depends on secure, industrial-scale supply chains for components that, in many cases, do not yet exist at scale anywhere in the world.

Building on Proxima’s existing partnerships across the supply chain, including for high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets, the agreement with Kyoto Fusioneering adds key building blocks of that supply chain: the systems that heat and fuel the plasma.

The agreement brings together Japan’s long standing expertise in fusion engineering with Germany’s world-leading stellarator research and industrial capabilities. It also strengthens industrial ties between the two countries as governments and companies worldwide race to turn fusion science into a new source of firm, dispatchable and clean energy.

The partnership will support Proxima’s roadmap towards Alpha, its demonstration stellarator planned for the early 2030s, and Stellaris, its first commercial fusion power plant.

]]> Autofixer, a Polish online car parts platform, has raised €3 million in venture debt financing to expand further across Europe, develop its platform and grow its team.

The financing came from Orbit Capital, a growth-stage venture debt and growth equity firm, whose portfolio includes Preply, Booksy, MEWS, Rohlik, among others. The venture debt financing allows Autofixer to access capital without diluting existing shareholders.

“The company’s rapid growth and strong business metrics demonstrate both clear product-market fit and the effectiveness of its business model. At this stage, venture debt is a natural way to support further growth, providing additional capital to scale the business without diluting existing shareholders,” said Wiktor Namysł, General Partner at Orbit Capital.

Autofixer was founded in 2021 by the team behind Renee and born2be, two e-commerce brands that were later consolidated under AZA Group. The group generated approximately €114 million in annual revenue at its peak, and the founders are bringing that expertise to the automotive parts market. The earlier growth was backed by Montis Capital, which invested in the company in both 2023 and 2025.

The premise is simple: buying car parts online is harder than it looks. The 360 million vehicles in Europe require a wide range of components, and even within a single model, parts can differ significantly across production years and trim levels. Another problem being that parts that look alike are not always interchangeable, while the information needed to identify the right component remains scattered across manufacturers and distributors.

Autofixer, as the name clearly implies, fixes this problem by combining vehicle data with parts catalogues, supplier listings, and records of previous part-to-vehicle matches. Autofixer’s platform relies on automation and AI to organise product descriptions and part numbers, helping drivers find components that are compatible with their specific cars.

“For a driver, buying the wrong part means more than returning a product. It means starting the search again and delaying the repair. We want to help drivers make an informed choice before placing an order. We bring together information about their car and the available parts so they can choose the right product without having to search through and compare multiple catalogues themselves,” said Szymon Jezierski, CEO of Autofixer.

The platform is not only designed for vehicle owners but also distributors, who can expand into new European markets without having to build a full e-commerce operation in each country. Autofixer integrates distributor listings and handles customer acquisition, marketing, and customer service.

In the first ten months of 2026, Autofixer processed more than 840k orders and expects to cross one million by the end of the year. The company has generated approximately €41 million in revenue so far this year, with full-year revenue expected to reach around €52 million. Since July, the company has recorded positive monthly EBITDA.

The €3 million will support Autofixer’s continued expansion in Europe, with Czechia as the next market and sales expected to begin within a month. The company also plans to use the fund to improve its platform technology and grow the team.

“The financing from Orbit Capital gives us the resources for our next stage of growth. We will invest in improving the platform, expanding our team and entering more European markets. As sales grow, we want to make the shopping experience more convenient for drivers too,” Jezierski added.

Autofixer plans to build AI-powered tools that guide drivers through the parts-selection process, as well as a companion app designed to support day-to-day car ownership.

]]> Querio, a London-based analytics platform for data teams and their AI agents, has launched today with €4.48 million ($5 million) in total funding. 

Its investors include BMW i Ventures, which led the company’s Seed financing, alongside LAUNCH, the fund run by Jason Calacanis, Haatch Ventures, Araya, Forum Ventures, and Secways.

“Companies want to use AI with their data, but they need to trust the answer. Querio lets data teams hand more of the work to AI agents while a person stays in charge of every change that reaches the business,” said Javier Bonilla, co-founder and CTO at Querio. 

Founded in 2024 by Rami Abi Habib (CEO) and Bonilla (CTO), Querio is an AI analytics platform that helps data teams give the whole company consistent answers in the AI tools it already uses. It keeps a company’s reports, definitions, and analysis in the data team’s GitHub and claims to give business users consistent answers in Claude, ChatGPT, and Slack, with the data team reviewing every change. 

According to the company, it was launched to address the growing challenge of keeping answers consistent across tools as employees turn to AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT for business questions. 

It says that when each tool uses a different version of the company’s numbers, people get conflicting answers, and data teams spend their time reconciling them instead of doing new work.

Querio claims to give data teams one place to define what the company’s numbers mean, and keeps that work in the team’s own GitHub rather than locked inside a vendor’s product. 

“For thirty years, analytics tools have kept a company’s logic inside the vendor’s product, where it’s hard to move and hard for AI to work with. Now everyone is asking data questions in Claude, Slack and wherever else they work, and they get three different revenue numbers. We built Querio so the data team owns that logic, and every AI tool in the company answers from it,” said Abi Habib, co-founder and CEO of Querio. 

The UK startup highlighted that business users can ask questions in Claude, ChatGPT or Slack and get the same answer each time. It further notes that when the business changes, Querio’s AI agent updates the affected reports and definitions, and the data team approves each change before anyone sees it.

“Say sales renames a field in the CRM. The revenue dashboard breaks, the Slack bot says no deals closed last week and Claude gives a third number. With Querio, the agent spots the change, fixes everything that depends on it and sends the data team one update to approve. After that, every tool gives the same answer,” Abi Habib added.

Querio is SOC 2 Type II certified and HIPAA- and GDPR-compliant. It also said it does not train on customer data and maintains no-training and no-storage agreements with its AI model providers. It works with companies including OpenVPN and agree.com.

This latest agreement also follows Impress’s over €110 million financing announcement in 2024, which supported its European expansion following the acquisition of DrSmile.

Impress’s financing comes amid a series of European investments in digital dentistry and AI-enabled healthcare in 2026.

In France, Paris-based DentalMonitoring secured €84 million to expand its AI-powered orthodontic monitoring platform, while Montpellier-based Lupin Dental raised €15 million for dental robotics. Belgium’s Relu also attracted €1.51 million for AI-powered dental workflows.

In Spain, Madrid-based Tucuvi raised €17 million for its voice-AI healthcare platform, while Barcelona’s Health Force secured €4.2 million for hospital automation.

Together with Impress’s €40 million venture debt loan, these announcements represent approximately €161.7 million in reported financing, spanning equity investments and debt.

“The digital transformation of the healthcare sector offers significant opportunities to improve the quality and efficiency of services provided to citizens. This operation reflects the EIB’s commitment to supporting innovative European growth companies like Impress that leverage AI to build cutting-edge solutions and expand their footprint across Europe, reinforcing EU leadership in HealthTech innovation,” adds María Romano, Head of the EIB Group Office in Spain.

Founded in Barcelona in 2019 by Vladimir Lupenko, Diliara Lupenko and Khaled Kasem, Impress is an invisible orthodontics and medical technology company. They offer a model that combines in-person care in specialised clinics with continuous monitoring through its AI-powered technology platform.

The company currently operates in 10 countries across Europe and the United States, with more than 110 clinics and 500,000 patients treated globally. In Spain, it has 22 clinics.

On the technology front, today’s investment will drive the development of Impress’s proprietary platform, a comprehensive AI-based healthcare ecosystem designed to unify patient treatment from start to finish.

The solution spans from in-clinic 3D intraoral scans – delivering more accurate tooth-movement predictions than traditional molds – AI-assisted treatment planning to ongoing patient tracking via Impress’s proprietary mobile app.

Its recent innovations include the industry’s first autonomous smile simulator, which uses artificial intelligence to recreate the “before and after” of treatment in just three seconds, with no need for manual intervention.

Having consolidated its position in Southern Europe, with Spain, Portugal and Italy as its main markets, Impress is preparing a new phase of international expansion focused on Northern Europe.

This strategy will focus mainly on the German, Dutch and UK markets, where the company has operated since 2023.

This growth plan is supported by the company’s strong performance over the last year, in which it posted positive EBITDA and 32% revenue growth, reaching €103 million. For 2026, Impress expects to reach revenue of around €145 million, representing growth of 40%.

The post “Bodyguard” satellites move closer to reality as UK awards Astroscale £15m contract appeared first on AGN.

]]> The UK has unveiled a £15 million ($20 million) defence contract with Astroscale to develop spacecraft capabilities for countering threats in orbit, as countries from the United States to Japan and India step up efforts to protect satellites from potentially hostile approaches.

Announced on 28 October, the contract places Astroscale UK in charge of Project LEDA, a Ministry of Defence programme intended to improve the country’s ability to understand and respond to spacecraft operating close to critical satellites.

BAE Systems and Open Cosmos will support the programme, which comes amid growing concern over Russian and Chinese satellites manoeuvring near other countries’ space assets.

The contract was signed on 29 September but publicly announced on Wednesday. It covers the manufacture, launch and operation of spacecraft intended to advance the UK’s understanding of orbital warfare and how to counter threatening rendezvous and proximity operations.

Tony Williams, head of space capability at UK Space Command, said the programme was about protecting the services on which the country depends rather than provoking confrontation in orbit.

“Control of space is not about seeking conflict in space, it is about demonstrating that we can protect the capabilities upon which our economy, our society, and our armed forces depend,” Williams said.

He added that LEDA would help the UK understand how manoeuvrable spacecraft could be used against threats involving other satellites approaching without permission.

The announcement follows a wider push by governments to develop what are increasingly being called bodyguard satellites or spacecraft designed to watch over valuable satellites, investigate suspicious activity and potentially intervene before an approaching object can cause damage.

From watching satellites to protecting them

For decades, space surveillance has largely involved tracking satellites and debris from the ground. But a new generation of manoeuvrable spacecraft could bring that monitoring much closer to the object being protected.

A bodyguard satellite might patrol near military communications or intelligence spacecraft, photograph an approaching object and move into position if its behaviour appears threatening.

Some proposed systems go further, using robotic arms or other mechanisms to capture and move an intruding satellite.

The distinction between surveillance and intervention is important. Technologies developed to inspect, refuel or remove spacecraft can also be used to interfere with them.

That concern was illustrated earlier this month when Russia’s Kosmos-2612 spacecraft approached ICEYE-X36, a radar imaging satellite operated by Finland-headquartered ICEYE.

Independent orbital observations indicated that the Russian spacecraft came within roughly one to two kilometres of ICEYE-X36, with some assessments suggesting a closer encounter.

ICEYE’s satellite network provides imagery that can support Ukraine’s defence. The approach raised concerns about possible surveillance or interference, although there is no publicly established evidence that Russia attempted to damage the spacecraft.

Russian Luch satellites have also conducted proximity operations near Western communications satellites in geostationary orbit, where many valuable military and commercial spacecraft operate.

The Secure World Foundation’s 2026 Global Counterspace Capabilities Report identifies growing interest in manoeuvrable satellites and orbital bodyguards as governments seek ways to respond to such activity.

UK programme gives Astroscale a defence role

Astroscale’s new contract follows several years of work on technologies that allow spacecraft to approach and operate near other objects in orbit.

Its ELSA-d mission demonstrated rendezvous and magnetic capture techniques, while ADRAS-J approached and inspected an abandoned Japanese rocket stage in 2024, coming within 15 metres.

The company says this experience provides a foundation for defence missions involving rendezvous and proximity operations.

Nick Shave, Astroscale UK’s managing director, said the protection of space infrastructure had become a concern extending well beyond the military.

“Resilience in space matters to everyone. The satellites we depend on support our armed forces, our economy and the services we use every day,” he said in the 28 October announcement.

“Our ambition is to be the trusted partner for Space Control.”

Earlier this month, Astroscale’s head of defence, Alex Godfrey, told Space.com that the company believed it could develop a bodyguard spacecraft ready for launch within three years.

Godfrey argued that many of the technical challenges involved in approaching another spacecraft had already been addressed through orbital servicing missions.

He also proposed a shared European patrol fleet, with protective satellites positioned to monitor groups of allied spacecraft rather than each country deploying individual escorts.

The LEDA contract is a significant development for Astroscale’s UK defence business, although the Ministry of Defence has not publicly described it as an order for an operational bodyguard fleet.

The UK is investing more broadly in space security. In September, the RAF established No. III Space Effects Squadron to counter hostile activity threatening UK satellites, including through electronic warfare.

The government has also committed £880 million ($1.2 billion) between 2026–27 and 2029–30 to space-based intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and space control activities.

US, France, Japan and India pursue similar capabilities

The United States already operates spacecraft capable of approaching and inspecting other satellites through the Space Force’s Geosynchronous Space Situational Awareness Program.

Its Victus Haze programme is also testing responsive spacecraft operations, including rendezvous and proximity manoeuvres relevant to identifying and responding to potential threats.

France is pursuing its YODA demonstration programme and the planned EGIDE follow-on capability, alongside Toutatis experiments involving surveillance and intervention in low Earth orbit.

Germany has also identified the need for manoeuvrable spacecraft to strengthen the protection of its space assets.

Japan’s Ministry of Defense set out similar priorities in its July 2025 Space Domain Defense Guidelines, calling for improved threat detection, satellite protection and the development of spacecraft capable of manoeuvring near other objects.

India, meanwhile, is reportedly working with private startups on more direct intervention technologies.

According to reports, Indian security agencies have discussed developing bodyguard satellites equipped with robotic arms to capture or move threatening spacecraft. Another proposed design would enclose smaller intruding satellites before moving them away.

The initiative follows a reported close encounter involving an Indian satellite in 2024 and growing concern over the military importance of space-based intelligence following India’s confrontation with Pakistan in 2025.

The post Lufthansa and Fraport trial ‘Gate of the Future’ at Frankfurt Airport appeared first on AGN.

]]> Lufthansa and Frankfurt Airport have showcased their so-called Gate of the Future, a redesigned departure gate that will act as a testbed for new technology and boarding processes at Germany’s primary hub. 

Located at Gate A16 in Terminal 1, the facility – launched by airport operator Fraport – combines real-time flight information, mobile boarding staff and lounge-style seating. 

Lufthansa and Fraport will use the trial to assess which features could be introduced at other gates across Frankfurt Airport – and potentially other airports in the future.

Digital services and mobile staff change how boarding gate will function

The redesigned gate is a refreshed take on the conventional departure lounge layout with a more flexible space intended to accommodate passengers working, relaxing or preparing to board.

Large displays provide departure times, boarding status, baggage information and live notifications of gate changes. 

Passengers can also scan QR codes to access digital services, including the Lufthansa mobile app.

Read more: 10 aircraft cabin innovations transforming the future of air travel Read more: 10 aircraft cabin innovations transforming the future of air travel

One significant change means that gate staff are no longer located behind a fixed counter.

Instead, they can move freely throughout the gate area, using tablets to access boarding systems and assist customers.

Fraport said the new approach was intended to make support more accessible while allowing staff to deal with a range of requests, including seat changes, upgrades and rebookings. 

Francesco Sciortino, board member at Lufthansa Airlines and hub manager for Frankfurt Airport, said the new design was aimed at creating a “premium passenger experience” with a “more pleasant and efficient start to their journey”.

Frankfurt Airport tests future gate design

Gate A16 features sofas, flexible workstations and enclosed “work cubes” providing private spaces to relax or work, giving the area a more lounge-like atmosphere than a conventional boarding gate.

However, Lufthansa and Fraport will not necessarily replicate the entire design elsewhere.

Feedback from the trial will help the two companies identify which features deliver the greatest benefits and are suitable for wider deployment.

Fraport Chief Operating Officer Dietmar Focke said: “The future of travel is emerging not in the laboratory but in actual operation. 

“Together with Lufthansa, we’re demonstrating how a strong partnership can generate specific innovations that noticeably enhance the travel experience. 

“What we’re testing and developing here together has a clear goal: greater comfort and convenience for passengers, optimised processes and an even stronger competitive position for Frankfurt as an aviation hub.”

]]> Indian startup Nalwa Aero has successfully flight-tested its scaled box-wing electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, demonstrating hovering and forward flight using electric propulsion and an all-tilting-rotor system.

The tests mark the first successful flights of the company’s unconventional aircraft design, which it hopes to develop into a five-seat platform for passenger transport, air ambulances and cargo operations.

The company, based in India’s northern state of Punjab, said the preliminary trials demonstrated that its unusual wing arrangement could support both vertical and forward flight, an important early step towards developing a full-sized aircraft.

Unlike most emerging electric air taxis, Nalwa Aero is pursuing a box-wing configuration in which the front and rear wings are connected at their tips, creating a closed structure around the aircraft. The design is intended to improve aerodynamic efficiency while providing the structural strength needed for a relatively large electric aircraft.

Founder and chief executive Kuljeet Singh Sandhu announced the successful flights on LinkedIn, describing the achievement as the culmination of years of development, setbacks and redesigns.

“They said it was impossible. We believed otherwise. Today, we made it fly!”, Sandhu wrote.

“We believe this represents a WORLD-FIRST achievement – successfully demonstrating an electric Box-Wing eVTOL aircraft with this unique all-tilting-rotor configuration, not previously achieved anywhere in the world, to this scale.”

The company has not disclosed the precise dimensions of the scaled aircraft, the number of flights completed or the duration of the trials. The demonstration remains an early development milestone rather than a flight of the proposed passenger-carrying aircraft.

India’s Civil Aviation Minister K. Ram Mohan Naidu welcomed the development after meeting Sandhu and Nalwa Aero chief technology officer Nelson Salas, who briefed him on the company’s progress.

“With such deep-tech innovations, we can transform urban mobility through flying taxis, air ambulances and even cargo flights, opening up exciting new possibilities!” the minister said.

What makes Nalwa Aero’s aircraft different?

The company’s aircraft draws on an aerodynamic concept explored more than a century ago by German scientist Ludwig Prandtl, whose research helped establish the foundations of modern aerodynamics.

A conventional aircraft generally has a single main wing, with a separate tailplane providing stability and control. Nalwa Aero’s box-wing arrangement uses two lifting surfaces connected at their outer ends.

The configuration is intended to reduce some of the aerodynamic losses associated with conventional wings, particularly the vortices generated at their tips. It could also provide structural advantages by distributing loads through the connected wings.

For an electric aircraft, aerodynamic efficiency is particularly important because battery weight and energy storage remain major limitations on range.

Nalwa Aero says preliminary internal studies suggest its design could deliver up to 40% greater aerodynamic efficiency than selected conventional aircraft configurations.

That figure has not yet been independently validated through full-scale flight testing. The company has described it as a potential improvement in certain aerodynamic parameters, rather than a demonstrated 40% increase in aircraft range.

The second unusual feature is the propulsion system.

Nalwa Aero’s proposed full-sized aircraft uses eight tilting rotors distributed across its front and rear wings. These provide vertical thrust for take-off and landing before changing orientation to propel the aircraft forwards.

In simple terms, the aircraft is designed to lift off like a helicopter and then fly forwards using its wings to generate lift.

This transition is one of the most demanding parts of tiltrotor aircraft development. The flight-control system must manage changing airflow and forces as the rotors tilt and the wings progressively take over the job of supporting the aircraft.

The successful demonstration of hovering and forward flight on the scaled model gives Nalwa Aero an opportunity to evaluate how the configuration behaves outside computer simulations.

However, the company has not specified whether the trials included a complete transition between vertical and wing-borne flight.

A five-seat aircraft with ambitious performance targets

Nalwa Aero is developing a larger aircraft under its Aphulas programme, with plans for passenger, emergency medical, cargo and defence applications.

The company lists a maximum take-off weight of 4,000 kg and a payload capacity of 1,000 kg for the proposed platform.

Its published performance targets include a cruising speed of 350 km/h, an all-electric range of 450 km and an endurance of approximately 90 minutes.

The company also envisages a hybrid hydrogen-powered version capable of travelling more than 1,500 km.

The aircraft is also intended to incorporate fly-by-wire flight controls, autonomous capabilities and flight-envelope protection. Fly-by-wire systems replace direct mechanical connections between the pilot’s controls and the aircraft’s control surfaces with electronic commands processed by computers.

Nalwa Aero says the platform could be reconfigured for different missions, including carrying passengers, transporting patients, delivering cargo and supporting emergency response operations.

For countries such as India, the company sees potential applications in regions where road journeys are slow or where conventional aviation infrastructure is limited.

What happens before an aircraft’s first flight?

Although the moment an experimental aircraft leaves the ground attracts the most attention, much of the work takes place before it ever flies.

Engineers developing a new aircraft must first establish whether its structure, propulsion system and flight controls will behave as expected.

The process normally begins with extensive computer modelling, including aerodynamic simulations and structural calculations.

For a design such as Nalwa Aero’s, engineers will evaluate how the connected wings carry loads, how airflow changes around the tilting rotors and how the aircraft responds when thrust is redirected.

Structural testing is used to establish whether wings, joints and other components can withstand expected flight loads.

Ground vibration testing can then help engineers identify the natural frequencies at which different parts of an aircraft vibrate. This is particularly important because certain combinations of aerodynamic forces and structural vibration can produce flutter, a potentially destructive phenomenon.

Flight-control systems also undergo extensive testing before they are trusted in the air.

Engineers commonly use hardware-in-the-loop simulations, feeding artificial flight conditions into the control computers to see how they respond to changes in attitude, wind and equipment failures.

For an electric tiltrotor aircraft, particular attention is paid to the motors, batteries, power distribution and the mechanisms that rotate the propulsion units.

Ground runs allow engineers to check motor performance, electrical loads, cooling and vibration while the aircraft remains secured.

Before the first flight, the development team also reviews test results, resolves significant anomalies and establishes the conditions under which the aircraft can be flown safely.

The company’s successful preliminary flights nevertheless provide the first reported airborne evidence that its experimental configuration can generate controlled vertical and forward flight.

Founder recalls years of setbacks

For Sandhu, the first flights carried particular significance after years spent developing the aircraft.

In his LinkedIn announcement, he recalled leaving Canada to pursue the project in India and described the difficulties the team encountered.

“A century-old aerodynamic vision. Years of failures, sacrifices, and perseverance. And today, a historic milestone for Indian aviation,” he wrote.

Sandhu said CTO Salas, who has more than 28 years of aircraft development experience, also relocated from the United States to India with his family to join the programme.

“We faced failures, doubts, financial challenges, redesigns, and countless sleepless nights,” Sandhu said.

“And when I watched our aircraft lift off the ground, I didn’t just see a machine flying. I saw every failure, every sleepless night, every sacrifice, and every reason we refused to give up,” Sandhu said.

Nalwa Aero is registered under India’s Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade and says its aircraft systems are being designed and developed domestically.

The company is pursuing both civilian and tactical applications, with a particular emphasis on aircraft capable of operating without conventional runways.

Regulatory approval and the road ahead

Nalwa Aero says it received Design Organisation Approval from India’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) in June 2025 for eVTOL aircraft in the five-seat-and-above category.

Its application for type certification was subsequently accepted in January 2026.

These steps allow the company to advance through the regulatory development process, but they do not mean the proposed passenger aircraft has been certified to enter service.

Before commercial operations can begin, Nalwa Aero will need to demonstrate the safety and performance of its full-sized design through further ground and flight testing.

That includes validating its propulsion system, flight controls, batteries, structural integrity and handling characteristics across the aircraft’s intended operating envelope.

The company has not yet announced a confirmed date for the first flight of its full-scale aircraft or a timetable for certification and commercial deliveries.

The post US F-16 fighters set to carry new hypersonic Blackbeard missile appeared first on AGN.

]]> The US Air Force has awarded a contract to integrate the new, low-cost Blackbeard hypersonic missile into its large F-16 fleet. The USAF and Navy are currently racing to develop and integrate multiple hypersonic missiles into their fighter jets amid a wider race with China and other countries.

Air Force follows Navy to integrate Castelion onto F-16 fleet

Yesterday, the US defence-tech company, Castelion, posted that it “has been awarded a contract modification to its existing work with the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin Blackbeard integration activities with the F-16.”

No value, timeline, or other details were provided, although it builds on earlier Air Force and AFRL investments that had totaled at least $37.2 million by September. This was for the continued development of Blackbeard, a low-cost, mass-producible hypersonic missile. Work for these prior contracts runs through June 2028.

The F-16 is a US Air Force 4th-generation workhorse that doesn’t need to carry munitions internally like the F-35 to preserve its stealth profile. Its ability to carry missiles externally makes integration more straightforward. That said, current USAF Blackbeard work also covers F-35A compatibility.

Castelion has been awarded a contract modification to its existing work with the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin Blackbeard integration activities with the F-16. We are grateful to the Air Force for their trust. Aim High. https://t.co/UerIcDG6Jx

— Castelion (@Castelion) October 26, 2026

Castelion is a venture capital-backed defence startup founded in 2022. The decision to integrate the missile into the Fighting Falcon fleet heralds a major step in the Air Force’s effort to incorporate hypersonic missiles onto its platforms.

The announcement comes as the Air Force also awarded a $694 million contract to Lockheed Martin to commence production of the hypersonic Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon.

The USAF’s current hypersonic weapons portfolio includes Castelion’s Blackbeard, Lockheed Martin’s AGM-183A ARRW and the Raytheon/Northrop Grumman Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM), although the three weapons occupy different roles.

Castelion’s new low-cost Blackbeard hypersonic missile

The high cost of many hypersonic weapons has been a major obstacle to procuring them in large numbers and limits their practical use cases to high-value and generally time-sensitive targets.

Affordability and production capacity are important elements of the Pentagon’s approach to make hypersonic missiles practical for a greater depth of use cases.

Blackbeard is being developed as a hypersonic, low-cost rocket-powered, boost-glide strike weapon with a nearly 500-mile strike range.

Castelion claims it is being designed for both maritime and land targets and promises to “significantly increase magazine depth and expand the lethal reach of naval aviation.”

Blackbeard has been developed with investment from the US Navy, US Army, and US Air Force, as well as with private investment. Its development includes vertical integration and commercial manufacturing methods to allow Castelion to better control the cost of producing the missiles.

The missiles are to be built at Castelion’s facility in Rio Rancho, New Mexico.

Australian startup Hypersonix raises Series A funding for reusable scramjet tech Australian startup Hypersonix raises Series A funding for reusable scramjet tech

Interest from the US Navy

The Air Force contract is not the first the company has received for its Blackbeard missile. In September, it reported it had received a production delivery order from the US Navy, with a total value of up to $200 million, to manufacture, assemble, test, and deliver an initial lot of Blackbeard Hypersonic Weapons.

The Air and Space Forces Magazine reports that the Navy is seeking to integrate the missile with its fleet of F/A-18 Super Hornets. The Navy’s Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23 conducted carriage and separation tests of the new missile in September, validating its compatibility with the fighter jet.

Blackbeard is going into production. The U.S. Navy has awarded Castelion a production order valued at up to $200 million for an initial lot of Blackbeard Hypersonic Weapons, following the 50 EOC rounds ordered in June. Engineered from day one for the production line. Grateful to PAE(A) for the trust and the urgency. https://t.co/qyAnQa0crz

— Castelion (@Castelion) September 14, 2026

Castelion also won a $105 million contract to integrate Blackbeard into the Super Hornets in April 2026. In June, the Navy signed a contract worth $23.4 million for 50 early operational capability pre-production prototype Blackbeard missiles.

Meanwhile, the US Army is funding development, integration, and testing of a ground-launched version (Blackbeard GL). This is to be compatible with existing HIMARS (M142) launchers as an interim solution.

]]> Atlantic Airways orders two more A320neos with Paris and London expansion in sight https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/exclusive-atlantic-airways-a320neos-london-paris/ Wed, 28 Oct 2026 12:30:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54726 Faroe Islands carrier Atlantic Airways has ordered two more A320neos, aiming for an all-neo fleet and additional flights to Paris and London.

The post Atlantic Airways orders two more A320neos with Paris and London expansion in sight appeared first on AGN.

]]> On Tuesday, Airbus announced that Faroe Islands flag carrier Atlantic Airways had signed a deal for two additional A320neo aircraft, bringing its total commitment for the type to six. Two of those have already been delivered, currently operating alongside an older-generation pair of A320ceos.

The latest addition to the order forms part of the carrier’s fleet expansion plans, allowing it to bolster frequencies on core routes, meet growing travel demand for outbound and inbound tourism from the Faroe Islands, and better connect to hubs that are key for feeder traffic with its airline partners.

Atlantic Airways is modernising its fleet

It hopes to transition to an all-A320neo fleet in the 2030s. It has two A320neos expected for delivery in 2028 and 2029, allowing it to replace (and slightly uplift) existing capacity with its ceo fleet.

The delivery timeline for the A320neo order announced on Tuesday has not yet been set.

“We are going for the most sustainable solution for our size,” CEO Jóhanna á Bergi told Aerospace Global News in an interview on Wednesday. “That means we are acquiring neo aircraft, and we have had an ambition over many years that by 2030, or in the early 2030s, we should be fully neo.”

“We are a very small company, but we have an important task: connecting our islands. It is critical infrastructure. Of course, we also want a modern means of transport, and for us the Airbus neo is a perfect fit.”

The carrier’s fleet choice is limited by the runway length (1799m) at its Vágar Airport hub. “We have looked at the A321 and so on,” á Bergi said, but “concluded that the A320 is a perfect match if you want to use the full capacity and also have the range.”

It hopes to have a clearer picture of the phase-in and phase-out dates of its new A320neos and A320ceos respectively early next year.

Atlantic Airways eyes more flights to London and Paris

Atlantic Airways hopes to use the additional capacity primarily to expand existing routes. The CEO identified Paris and London as destinations it hopes to grow. It currently serves both summer-seasonally and anticipates moving them to year-round operations.

Last year, the airline transported just under 380,000 passengers on scheduled flights, 12% more than in 2019. Non-Faroe Island residents made up 50% of its business for the first time this year.

Its main scheduled business is primarily concentrated in the summer season. “If you look now in November, December, January, February, we have maybe 25 to 30 departures per week. And if you’re in the high season, we have more than 60 departures.”

For its size, Atlantic Airways’ network is quite vast. Its operation spans 13 destinations which á Bergi describes as “a lot for our small society.” The Faroe Islands is home to about 55,000 people.

Introducing additional frequencies to Paris will also serve traffic looking to fly onwards with its partner carriers.

“At the moment we have three flights per week to Paris, and it looks very good in cooperation with Air France-KLM and so on.”

Milan and London are also useful for feeder traffic purposes, á Bergi says. Milan Malpensa (MXP) will join the network next summer.

As for its core destinations in Scandinavia, the CEO says that there is “sufficient capacity” but added that subject to demand, its operations could be expanded further down the line. Given that the Faroe Islands are part of the Kingdom of Denmark, the links between the two are of particular importance. Denmark accounts for roughly 50% of its traffic.

Should it finally get slots in Amsterdam – something it has been eyeing for some time – it would also deploy capacity to the Netherlands, capturing feeder demand via partner KLM.

No to New York – for now

Atlantic Airways used to operate an Airbus A320 flight to New York Stewart International Airport for a limited time in the summer in both 2023 and 2024. Only 150 seats out of the 174 total were available for use given the distance.

Demand was lower than expected, and after just two seasons in operation, the airline pulled the route. When asked, the CEO says that there are no plans “in the short run” to reintroduce New York.

“The short story about New York is that we are a small airline with narrow-body aircraft, we don’t have a long runway, and we fully utilise our aircraft. We did it [launching New York] because we could, and we tried it.”

The A320s took roughly six hours to complete each leg. “We think we can do other things better, or more sensibly, in Europe. If you go to the US, you are away with your aircraft for a day or two. If you fly in Europe, you can do several trips. With our very small fleet, at the moment we are concentrating on Europe.”

Passengers looking to fly from the Faroe Islands to North America can do so via Reykjavík through codeshare partner Icelandair.

Atlantic Airways now competes against 3 new players in the Faroe Islands

Traffic to the Faroe Islands has grown considerably in recent years, driven primarily by Atlantic Airways. However, new players have also entered the market. Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) introduced flights to Copenhagen in 2017, Widerøe to Bergen in 2021 and Icelandair to Reykjavík in 2024.

“It’s like everywhere else in that you are both working and are good together and you’re also competing,” á Bergi responded when asked whether the company views the additional capacity as a threat. She highlighted that new players provide customers with the freedom of choice, and that is something that “we just have to live with.”

It currently has a codeshare agreement with Icelandair, and “would really like to have” one with SAS.

Charter operations balance out lower demand in the winter season

During the winter, the carrier relies on its charter business to keep its aircraft and employees busy – and, crucially, ensure its bottom line stays positive.

Most of its charter flights operate from Denmark in collaboration with leisure experts Apollo and FolkeFerie. This includes flights to places like Malta which is “one of the big ones” alongside services to Greece and other places in the Mediterranean.

During the winter, the carrier also operates ski charters and transports different national teams. “We even had some military transport up to Greenland,” á Bergi revealed.

“So we do a lot of different ad hoc work, but we always serve the Faroese market first, and then we see where we have excess capacity. In that way, we optimise our business.”

]]> Where are the USAF’s retired KC-10 Extenders now – and how many could fly again? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/retired-usaf-kc10-extenders-omega-air/ Wed, 28 Oct 2026 12:20:58 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54770 The KC-10 may be gone from USAF service, but up to 14 retired Extenders could still return to the skies under new owners.

The post Where are the USAF’s retired KC-10 Extenders now – and how many could fly again? appeared first on AGN.

]]> The US Air Force retired its last KC-10 Extender in September 2024, ending more than four decades of KC-10 operations. While most retired KC-10 aircraft were sent to storage at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, several former USAF KC-10s could return to service with Omega Air or a North African military operator.

Ten former USAF tankers have been registered to private aerial refuelling company Omega Air. A separate proposal could see up to four more USAF aircraft transferred to a North African operator.

The renewed interest in the fate of the KC-10 fleet follows the return to flight of former USAF KC-10A 86-0034, now registered N82247, on 20 October 2026.

As AGN previously reported, the aircraft departed the 309th Aerospace Maintenance and Regeneration Group (AMARG) facility at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona and flew to San Antonio, Texas.

It was the first confirmed flight of a retired USAF KC-10 under civilian ownership. The aircraft had been in storage since May 2023.

Why was the KC-10 retired?

The KC-10 Extender was developed from the McDonnell Douglas DC-10 and entered USAF service in 1981. The tanker combined strategic airlift capability with aerial refuelling, allowing it to support long-range combat and transport operations worldwide.

The Air Force retired the KC-10 as part of its fleet modernisation programme, replacing the aircraft with the Boeing KC-46A Pegasus.

What happened to the USAF’s 59 surviving KC-10 Extenders?

The USAF received 60 McDonnell Douglas KC-10A Extenders between 1979 and 1987. One aircraft was destroyed in a ground fire at Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana in 1987, leaving 59 in the fleet.

The USAF began retiring the KC-10 in 2020, as it introduced the Boeing KC-46A Pegasus. The final operational Extender departed Travis Air Force Base in California on 26 September 2024.

Most retired KC-10s were sent to AMARG at Davis-Monthan, where military aircraft are stored, maintained for potential future use, dismantled for parts or prepared for disposal.

Not every aircraft is in the same condition. Some have been stripped of equipment, while others have been preserved for possible restoration. A small number have also been retained for museum display.

Which ten former USAF KC-10s has Omega Air acquired?

Omega Air, a US company that provides contracted aerial refuelling services, acquired ten former USAF KC-10s following a government auction in 2025.

The US General Services Administration offered ten aircraft for sale in April 2025, with bidding closing on 6 May.

The aircraft were offered in non-flyable condition. Each was missing one wing-mounted engine and its aerial refuelling boom, which was removed to support the remaining USAF fleet.

The FAA aircraft registry identifies ten McDonnell Douglas DC-10-30F aircraft registered to Omega Air Inc., based in Selma, Texas, during September and October 2026.

The registrations and corresponding manufacturer serial numbers are:

Source: FAA aircraft registration records. Manufacturer serial numbers are distinct from USAF military serial numbers.

N82247 has been confirmed as former USAF KC-10A 86-0034. The remaining nine civilian registrations have not yet been independently matched to their former USAF tail numbers.

The FAA records confirm the aircraft are registered to Omega, but do not provide information on their airworthiness or whether they are being restored for operational service.

When will Omega Air’s KC-10 tankers return to service?

Omega already operates DC-10-derived aerial refuelling aircraft, including former Royal Netherlands Air Force KDC-10s. Its existing fleet provides an operational and maintenance base for the larger KC-10 programme.

The flight of N82247 on 20 October demonstrated that at least one retired KC-10 could be returned to flying condition after several years in storage.

However, the aircraft flew without its original aerial refuelling boom. Its return to flight does not mean it is ready to conduct operational refuelling missions.

Omega has not publicly confirmed a restoration schedule for the remaining nine aircraft, identified which aircraft will fly next or said how many it intends to return to commercial refuelling service.

The company could restore more aircraft or keep some for spare parts. 

Could four more KC-10 Extenders return to service in North Africa?

A separate US government proposal could see up to four retired KC-10s returned to military service for an unnamed North African operator.

On 7 October 2026, the US Air Force Life Cycle Management Centre issued a request for information seeking contractors capable of regenerating and supporting the aircraft.

The contracting notice, updated on 27 October, calls for aircraft restoration, depot-level maintenance, flight clearance, international delivery, crew and maintenance training, and contractor logistics support.

The proposed sustainment programme would run for three to five years.

The aircraft would be transferred under the US Excess Defence Articles programme, which allows surplus US military equipment to be supplied to foreign partners.

The prospective recipient has not been officially identified. Egypt and Morocco have been mentioned as possible candidates by the War Zone and other reports, but the US Air Force describes it only as a North African partner.

How many retired USAF KC-10s could eventually fly again?

Of the 59 KC-10s that survived their USAF careers, one is confirmed to have returned to flight under civilian ownership.

Omega’s ten-aircraft acquisition means at least some of these USAF KC-10 tankers could fly again. The North African proposal could restore up to four more aircraft to service.

However, the number of KC-10 tankers that will actually fly again is still unknown.

The aircraft have spent years in storage. Restoring them will require engines, maintenance work, replacement components and, for aerial refuelling operations, suitable refuelling equipment. The cost of that work could determine how many are restored and how many are scrapped for spare parts.

For now, N82247 is the only former USAF KC-10 confirmed to have flown again. The type’s future will depend on whether Omega returns another aircraft to flight and whether the USAF proceeds with the proposed North African transfer.

]]> Jet2 retires world’s oldest Boeing 737-800 after 29 years https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/jet2-retires-worlds-oldest-boeing-737-800/ Wed, 28 Oct 2026 11:30:49 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54741 Registered G-GDFD, the aircraft completed its final commercial flight on 18 October, operating flight LS644 from Ibiza to East Midlands Airport.

The post Jet2 retires world’s oldest Boeing 737-800 after 29 years appeared first on AGN.

]]> Jet2 has retired a 29-year-old Boeing 737-800, ending the flying career of the oldest aircraft of its type still in service worldwide.

Registered G-GDFD, the aircraft completed its final commercial flight on 18 October, operating flight LS644 from Ibiza to East Midlands Airport.  It was flown to Manchester the same day for de-branding and work ahead of its return to the lessor. 

Future of 29-year-old Boeing 737-800 unclear

Jet2 has not confirmed whether the aircraft will fly again, be preserved or be dismantled.

The aircraft, manufacturer serial number 27982, first flew on 15 August 1997. According to Airliner World, the airframe was only the second 737-800 prototype and the eighth aircraft built for Boeing’s Next Generation programme. 

It is now the oldest surviving example of the 737NG family, after the seven aircraft built before it were scrapped.

Initially registered N35030, the twinjet was used in Boeing’s flight-test programme before entering commercial service with German carrier Hapag-Lloyd in December 1998 as D-AHFB, according to PlaneSpotters.net. 

It subsequently operated for Hapagfly from 2005 to 2007 and TUIfly from 2007 – where it was painted in “VolksWagen Sharan” special colours – before joining Jet2 in April 2011.

Airframe accrued more than 80,000 flight hours

The airframe spent the final 15 years of its airline career with the British leisure airline, where it was painted with the white and blue sun livery promoting Jet2holidays. 

The aircraft accumulated more than 80,000 flight hours.

Its retirement comes as the leisure airline introduces Airbus A321neos as part of the renewal of its Boeing 737 fleet.

Over the summer, Jet2 took delivery of its 30th Airbus A321neo aircraft as part of Jet2’s firm order for 155 brand-new Airbus A321neo aircraft. 

Jet2 took delivery of its first-ever Airbus aircraft, an Airbus A321neo registered G-SUNB, in March 2023. 

The airline is also completing a multi-million pound Split Scimitar Winglet retrofit programme across 74 Boeing 737-800NG aircraft and applying lightweight paint to over 80 aircraft.

Read more: Jet2 scraps La Palma flights six months after launching Canary Islands route Read more: Jet2 scraps La Palma flights six months after launching Canary Islands route

Another Airbus retirement … of the A340-600

The departure of G-GDFD is one of two notable fleet retirements this month. 

Lufthansa operated its final scheduled Airbus A340-600 service last week, ending 23 years of flying the four-engined type.

Flight LH419 from Washington Dulles landed in Frankfurt after an eight-hour journey, with 267 passengers on board the aircraft, registered D-AIHW.

Lufthansa operated 24 A340-600s over the years. The 75.3m-long aircraft was the world’s longest passenger airliner when it entered service, and carried more than 40 million passengers for the German group, according to the airline.

Its retirement forms part of Lufthansa’s wider fleet renewal, with newer aircraft including the Airbus A350-1000 and Boeing 787 and 777-9 expected to replace older types. 

By 2028, Lufthansa expects next-generation aircraft to account for 70% of its long-haul fleet.

]]> First Boeing 737 MAX 10 rolls out of Everett factory in historic production milestone https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/first-boeing-737-max-10-rolls-out-everett-factory/ Wed, 28 Oct 2026 09:29:57 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54712 Boeing has completed the first 737 MAX 10 at its new Everett production line, marking the first time a 737 has rolled out of a factory outside Renton in more than five decades.

The post First Boeing 737 MAX 10 rolls out of Everett factory in historic production milestone appeared first on AGN.

]]> Boeing has rolled out the first 737 MAX 10 built at its new production line in Everett, Washington. It marks the first time a 737 has been completed outside Renton in more than 50 years.

The aircraft, destined for Canadian airline WestJet, emerged from Boeing’s North Line on Monday, 26 October, just six days after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) certified the largest 737 MAX aircraft.

According to The Seattle Times, the aircraft completed all scheduled assembly stations before moving to the factory apron at about 2 pm local time.

Seven other aircraft are currently progressing through the new production line, which opened in July 2026.

The rollout is an important step in Boeing’s efforts to increase 737 production and begin deliveries of the long-delayed MAX 10. However, the first aircraft still requires modifications before it can enter airline service.

Boeing builds first 737 outside Renton in over 50 years

Boeing officially opened the Everett North Line in July, converting part of a factory previously used to manufacture widebody aircraft.

The Everett site first opened in the 1960s to build the Boeing 747 and later became a major production centre for the 767, 777 and 787.

Until this year, Boeing had manufactured its 737 aircraft exclusively at Renton, which is approximately 40 miles south of Everett. It transferred narrowbody production to Renton in 1970.

The new facility adds a fourth 737 MAX final assembly line alongside the three existing lines at Renton.

Everett’s larger production space is particularly suited to the longer MAX 10. Aircraft can move through the North Line nose-to-tail. Production at Renton requires greater spacing between the larger jets.

Boeing invested around $1 billion in converting the Everett facility for narrowbody production.

The project was originally scheduled to begin operations nearly two years earlier, but it was delayed as Boeing addressed production and quality-control problems after the January 2024 Alaska Airlines 737 MAX 9 door-plug incident.

First WestJet 737 MAX 10 still requires modifications

Although the first Everett-built MAX 10 has completed final assembly, it is not yet ready for delivery.

The aircraft must undergo what Boeing calls change incorporation. Aircraft that were manufactured before FAA certification must be updated with design modifications developed during the certification process to meet the final approved design.

These include changes to the engine anti-ice system and an enhanced angle-of-attack sensor required by the FAA.

The aircraft will undergo preflight inspections before moving to another Boeing facility, potentially Moses Lake or Seattle, for the additional work. Boeing has not disclosed how long the modifications will take.

The FAA must also still approve production operations at the new North Line. That is a separate approval process from its certification of the MAX 10 aircraft type.

For now, Boeing is operating the Everett facility at a reduced production rate while workers establish and verify the assembly processes. The initial phase covers at least 10 aircraft.

As a result, the first MAX 10 to roll out of Everett may not be the first delivered to an airline.

New Everett line will support Boeing’s 737 production increase

The North Line is central to Boeing’s plans to increase monthly 737 MAX output. The manufacturer is working towards stabilising production at 42 aircraft per month before increasing to 47 and eventually 52.

Boeing expects Everett to provide the additional assembly capacity needed for higher production rates, while the Renton factory continues building other MAX variants.

The planemaker has said the additional line would also provide greater flexibility for aircraft that require extra production work or more complex cabin installations.

The company has a backlog of more than 4,000 737 MAX aircraft, with outstanding orders extending into the next decade.

The MAX 10 accounts for a substantial share of that demand. Aviation consultancy IBA estimated that airlines had ordered more than 1,550 aircraft, representing approximately 31% of Boeing’s outstanding 737 backlog, according to Reuters.

When will Boeing deliver the first 737 MAX 10?

The FAA certified the Boeing 737 MAX 10 on 20 October 2026, ending years of regulatory delays for the aircraft. Boeing now anticipates certification from Transport Canada and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency to follow the FAA’s approval.

The MAX 10 was originally expected to enter commercial service in 2020.

With capacity for up to 230 passengers, the aircraft is Boeing’s largest single-aisle jet and competes directly with the Airbus A321neo family. In a typical two-class configuration, the MAX 10 accommodates approximately 185 to 210 passengers and has a range of up to 3,100 nautical miles.

The larger cabin gives airlines more seating capacity to serve busy short- and medium-haul routes, reducing operating costs per seat compared with smaller aircraft.

WestJet is expected to receive its first MAX 10 in early 2027, subject to remaining regulatory and production requirements.

Other major MAX 10 customers waiting for their aircraft include United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Alaska Airlines, American Airlines and Ryanair.

The first Everett-built aircraft is now advancing to the final stages of preparation. Boeing’s next key production milestones will be securing FAA approval for the North Line and increasing its output as MAX 10 deliveries begin.
